The wise and orderly soul follows in the straight path and is conscious of her surroundings; but the soul which desires the body, and which, as I was relating before, has long been fluttering about the lifeless frame and the world of sight, is after many struggles and many sufferings hardly and with violence carried away by her attendant genius, and when she arrives at the place where the other souls are gathered, if she be impure and have done impure deeds, whether foul murders or other crimes which are the brothers of these, and the works of brothers in crime--from that soul every one flees and turns away; no one will be her companion, no one her guide, but alone she wanders in extremity of evil until certain times are fulfilled, and when they are fulfilled, she is borne irresistibly to her own fitting habitation; as every pure and just soul which has passed through life in the company and under the guidance of the gods has also her own proper home.
Now the earth has divers wonderful regions, and is indeed in nature and extent very unlike the notions of geographers, as I believe on the authority of one who shall be nameless.
What do you mean, Socrates? said Simmias. I have myself heard many descriptions of the earth, but I do not know, and I should very much like to know, in which of these you put faith.

And I, Simmias, replied Socrates, if I had the art of Glaucus would tell you; although I know not that the art of Glaucus could prove the truth of my tale, which I myself should never be able to prove, and even if I could, I fear, Simmias, that my life would come to an end before the argument was completed. I may describe to you, however, the form and regions of the earth according to my conception of them.
That, said Simmias, will be enough.

Well, then, he said, my conviction is, that the earth is a round body in the centre of the heavens, and therefore has no need of air or any similar force to be a support, but is kept there and hindered from falling or inclining any way by the equability of the surrounding heaven and by her own equipoise. For that which, being in equipoise, is in the centre of that which is equably diffused, will not incline any way in any degree, but will always remain in the same state and not deviate. And this is my first notion.
Which is surely a correct one, said Simmias.

Also I believe that the earth is very vast, and that we who dwell in the region extending from the river Phasis to the Pillars of Heracles inhabit a small portion only about the sea, like ants or frogs about a marsh, and that there are other inhabitants of many other like places; for everywhere on the face of the earth there are hollows of various forms and sizes, into which the water and the mist and the lower air collect. But the true earth is pure and situated in the pure heaven--there are the stars also; and it is the heaven which is commonly spoken of by us as the ether, and of which our own earth is the sediment gathering in the hollows beneath. But we who live in these hollows are deceived into the notion that we are dwelling above on the surface of the earth; which is just as if a creature who was at the bottom of the sea were to fancy that he was on the surface of the water, and that the sea was the heaven through which he saw the sun and the other stars, he having never come to the surface by reason of his feebleness and sluggishness, and having never lifted up his head and seen, nor ever heard from one who had seen, how much purer and fairer the world above is than his own. And such is exactly our case: for we are dwelling in a hollow of the earth, and fancy that we are on the surface; and the air we call the heaven, in which we imagine that the stars move. But the fact is, that owing to our feebleness and sluggishness we are prevented from reaching the surface of the air: for if any man could arrive at the exterior limit, or take the wings of a bird and come to the top, then like a fish who puts his head out of the water and sees this world, he would see a world beyond; and, if the nature of man could sustain the sight, he would acknowledge that this other world was the place of the true heaven and the true light and the true earth. For our earth, and the stones, and the entire region which surrounds us, are spoilt and corroded, as in the sea all things are corroded by the brine, neither is there any noble or perfect growth, but caverns only, and sand, and an endless slough of mud: and even the shore is not to be compared to the fairer sights of this world. And still less is this our world to be compared with the other. Of that upper earth which is under the heaven, I can tell you a charming tale, Simmias, which is well worth hearing.
And we, Socrates, replied Simmias, shall be charmed to listen to you.

The tale, my friend, he said, is as follows:--In the first place, the earth, when looked at from above, is in appearance streaked like one of those balls which have leather coverings in twelve pieces, and is decked with various colours, of which the colours used by painters on earth are in a manner samples. But there the whole earth is made up of them, and they are brighter far and clearer than ours; there is a purple of wonderful lustre, also the radiance of gold, and the white which is in the earth is whiter than any chalk or snow. Of these and other colours the earth is made up, and they are more in number and fairer than the eye of man has ever seen; the very hollows (of which I was speaking) filled with air and water have a colour of their own, and are seen like light gleaming amid the diversity of the other colours, so that the whole presents a single and continuous appearance of variety in unity. And in this fair region everything that grows--trees, and flowers, and fruits--are in a like degree fairer than any here; and there are hills, having stones in them in a like degree smoother, and more transparent, and fairer in colour than our highly-valued emeralds and sardonyxes and jaspers, and other gems, which are but minute fragments of them: for there all the stones are like our precious stones, and fairer still (compare Republic). The reason is, that they are pure, and not, like our precious stones, infected or corroded by the corrupt briny elements which coagulate among us, and which breed foulness and disease both in earth and stones, as well as in animals and plants. They are the jewels of the upper earth, which also shines with gold and silver and the like, and they are set in the light of day and are large and abundant and in all places, making the earth a sight to gladden the beholder's eye. And there are animals and men, some in a middle region, others dwelling about the air as we dwell about the sea; others in islands which the air flows round, near the continent: and in a word, the air is used by them as the water and the sea are by us, and the ether is to them what the air is to us. Moreover, the temperament of their seasons is such that they have no disease, and live much longer than we do, and have sight and hearing and smell, and all the other senses, in far greater perfection, in the same proportion that air is purer than water or the ether than air. Also they have temples and sacred places in which the gods really dwell, and they hear their voices and receive their answers, and are conscious of them and hold converse with them, and they see the sun, moon, and stars as they truly are, and their other blessedness is of a piece with this.

chapters.title: Rivers Under the Earth
paras: Such is the nature of the whole earth, and of the things which are around the earth; and there are divers regions in the hollows on the face of the globe everywhere, some of them deeper and more extended than that which we inhabit, others deeper but with a narrower opening than ours, and some are shallower and also wider. All have numerous perforations, and there are passages broad and narrow in the interior of the earth, connecting them with one another; and there flows out of and into them, as into basins, a vast tide of water, and huge subterranean streams of perennial rivers, and springs hot and cold, and a great fire, and great rivers of fire, and streams of liquid mud, thin or thick (like the rivers of mud in Sicily, and the lava streams which follow them), and the regions about which they happen to flow are filled up with them. And there is a swinging or see-saw in the interior of the earth which moves all this up and down, and is due to the following cause:--There is a chasm which is the vastest of them all, and pierces right through the whole earth; this is that chasm which Homer describes in the words,--
'Far off, where is the inmost depth beneath the earth;'

and which he in other places, and many other poets, have called Tartarus. And the see-saw is caused by the streams flowing into and out of this chasm, and they each have the nature of the soil through which they flow. And the reason why the streams are always flowing in and out, is that the watery element has no bed or bottom, but is swinging and surging up and down, and the surrounding wind and air do the same; they follow the water up and down, hither and thither, over the earth--just as in the act of respiration the air is always in process of inhalation and exhalation;--and the wind swinging with the water in and out produces fearful and irresistible blasts: when the waters retire with a rush into the lower parts of the earth, as they are called, they flow through the earth in those regions, and fill them up like water raised by a pump, and then when they leave those regions and rush back hither, they again fill the hollows here, and when these are filled, flow through subterranean channels and find their way to their several places, forming seas, and lakes, and rivers, and springs. Thence they again enter the earth, some of them making a long circuit into many lands, others going to a few places and not so distant; and again fall into Tartarus, some at a point a good deal lower than that at which they rose, and others not much lower, but all in some degree lower than the point from which they came. And some burst forth again on the opposite side, and some on the same side, and some wind round the earth with one or many folds like the coils of a serpent, and descend as far as they can, but always return and fall into the chasm. The rivers flowing in either direction can descend only to the centre and no further, for opposite to the rivers is a precipice.

Now these rivers are many, and mighty, and diverse, and there are four principal ones, of which the greatest and outermost is that called Oceanus, which flows round the earth in a circle; and in the opposite direction flows Acheron, which passes under the earth through desert places into the Acherusian lake: this is the lake to the shores of which the souls of the many go when they are dead, and after waiting an appointed time, which is to some a longer and to some a shorter time, they are sent back to be born again as animals. The third river passes out between the two, and near the place of outlet pours into a vast region of fire, and forms a lake larger than the Mediterranean Sea, boiling with water and mud; and proceeding muddy and turbid, and winding about the earth, comes, among other places, to the extremities of the Acherusian Lake, but mingles not with the waters of the lake, and after making many coils about the earth plunges into Tartarus at a deeper level. This is that Pyriphlegethon, as the stream is called, which throws up jets of fire in different parts of the earth. The fourth river goes out on the opposite side, and falls first of all into a wild and savage region, which is all of a dark-blue colour, like lapis lazuli; and this is that river which is called the Stygian river, and falls into and forms the Lake Styx, and after falling into the lake and receiving strange powers in the waters, passes under the earth, winding round in the opposite direction, and comes near the Acherusian lake from the opposite side to Pyriphlegethon. And the water of this river too mingles with no other, but flows round in a circle and falls into Tartarus over against Pyriphlegethon; and the name of the river, as the poets say, is Cocytus.

Such is the nature of the other world; and when the dead arrive at the place to which the genius of each severally guides them, first of all, they have sentence passed upon them, as they have lived well and piously or not. And those who appear to have lived neither well nor ill, go to the river Acheron, and embarking in any vessels which they may find, are carried in them to the lake, and there they dwell and are purified of their evil deeds, and having suffered the penalty of the wrongs which they have done to others, they are absolved, and receive the rewards of their good deeds, each of them according to his deserts. But those who appear to be incurable by reason of the greatness of their crimes--who have committed many and terrible deeds of sacrilege, murders foul and violent, or the like--such are hurled into Tartarus which is their suitable destiny, and they never come out. Those again who have committed crimes, which, although great, are not irremediable--who in a moment of anger, for example, have done violence to a father or a mother, and have repented for the remainder of their lives, or, who have taken the life of another under the like extenuating circumstances--these are plunged into Tartarus, the pains of which they are compelled to undergo for a year, but at the end of the year the wave casts them forth--mere homicides by way of Cocytus, parricides and matricides by Pyriphlegethon--and they are borne to the Acherusian lake, and there they lift up their voices and call upon the victims whom they have slain or wronged, to have pity on them, and to be kind to them, and let them come out into the lake. And if they prevail, then they come forth and cease from their troubles; but if not, they are carried back again into Tartarus and from thence into the rivers unceasingly, until they obtain mercy from those whom they have wronged: for that is the sentence inflicted upon them by their judges. Those too who have been pre-eminent for holiness of life are released from this earthly prison, and go to their pure home which is above, and dwell in the purer earth; and of these, such as have duly purified themselves with philosophy live henceforth altogether without the body, in mansions fairer still which may not be described, and of which the time would fail me to tell.
Wherefore, Simmias, seeing all these things, what ought not we to do that we may obtain virtue and wisdom in this life? Fair is the prize, and the hope great!

A man of sense ought not to say, nor will I be very confident, that the description which I have given of the soul and her mansions is exactly true. But I do say that, inasmuch as the soul is shown to be immortal, he may venture to think, not improperly or unworthily, that something of the kind is true. The venture is a glorious one, and he ought to comfort himself with words like these, which is the reason why I lengthen out the tale. Wherefore, I say, let a man be of good cheer about his soul, who having cast away the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien to him and working harm rather than good, has sought after the pleasures of knowledge; and has arrayed the soul, not in some foreign attire, but in her own proper jewels, temperance, and justice, and courage, and nobility, and truth--in these adorned she is ready to go on her journey to the world below, when her hour comes. You, Simmias and Cebes, and all other men, will depart at some time or other. Me already, as the tragic poet would say, the voice of fate calls. Soon I must drink the poison; and I think that I had better repair to the bath first, in order that the women may not have the trouble of washing my body after I am dead.

chapters.title: The Cup
paras: When he had done speaking, Crito said: And have you any commands for us, Socrates--anything to say about your children, or any other matter in which we can serve you?

Nothing particular, Crito, he replied: only, as I have always told you, take care of yourselves; that is a service which you may be ever rendering to me and mine and to all of us, whether you promise to do so or not. But if you have no thought for yourselves, and care not to walk according to the rule which I have prescribed for you, not now for the first time, however much you may profess or promise at the moment, it will be of no avail.
We will do our best, said Crito: And in what way shall we bury you?

In any way that you like; but you must get hold of me, and take care that I do not run away from you. Then he turned to us, and added with a smile:--I cannot make Crito believe that I am the same Socrates who have been talking and conducting the argument; he fancies that I am the other Socrates whom he will soon see, a dead body--and he asks, How shall he bury me? And though I have spoken many words in the endeavour to show that when I have drunk the poison I shall leave you and go to the joys of the blessed,--these words of mine, with which I was comforting you and myself, have had, as I perceive, no effect upon Crito. And therefore I want you to be surety for me to him now, as at the trial he was surety to the judges for me: but let the promise be of another sort; for he was surety for me to the judges that I would remain, and you must be my surety to him that I shall not remain, but go away and depart; and then he will suffer less at my death, and not be grieved when he sees my body being burned or buried. I would not have him sorrow at my hard lot, or say at the burial, Thus we lay out Socrates, or, Thus we follow him to the grave or bury him; for false words are not only evil in themselves, but they infect the soul with evil. Be of good cheer, then, my dear Crito, and say that you are burying my body only, and do with that whatever is usual, and what you think best.

When he had spoken these words, he arose and went into a chamber to bathe; Crito followed him and told us to wait. So we remained behind, talking and thinking of the subject of discourse, and also of the greatness of our sorrow; he was like a father of whom we were being bereaved, and we were about to pass the rest of our lives as orphans. When he had taken the bath his children were brought to him--(he had two young sons and an elder one); and the women of his family also came, and he talked to them and gave them a few directions in the presence of Crito; then he dismissed them and returned to us.

Now the hour of sunset was near, for a good deal of time had passed while he was within. When he came out, he sat down with us again after his bath, but not much was said. Soon the jailer, who was the servant of the Eleven, entered and stood by him, saying:--To you, Socrates, whom I know to be the noblest and gentlest and best of all who ever came to this place, I will not impute the angry feelings of other men, who rage and swear at me, when, in obedience to the authorities, I bid them drink the poison--indeed, I am sure that you will not be angry with me; for others, as you are aware, and not I, are to blame. And so fare you well, and try to bear lightly what must needs be--you know my errand. Then bursting into tears he turned away and went out.

Socrates looked at him and said: I return your good wishes, and will do as you bid. Then turning to us, he said, How charming the man is: since I have been in prison he has always been coming to see me, and at times he would talk to me, and was as good to me as could be, and now see how generously he sorrows on my account. We must do as he says, Crito; and therefore let the cup be brought, if the poison is prepared: if not, let the attendant prepare some.

Yet, said Crito, the sun is still upon the hill-tops, and I know that many a one has taken the draught late, and after the announcement has been made to him, he has eaten and drunk, and enjoyed the society of his beloved; do not hurry--there is time enough.

Socrates said: Yes, Crito, and they of whom you speak are right in so acting, for they think that they will be gainers by the delay; but I am right in not following their example, for I do not think that I should gain anything by drinking the poison a little later; I should only be ridiculous in my own eyes for sparing and saving a life which is already forfeit. Please then to do as I say, and not to refuse me.

Crito made a sign to the servant, who was standing by; and he went out, and having been absent for some time, returned with the jailer carrying the cup of poison. Socrates said: You, my good friend, who are experienced in these matters, shall give me directions how I am to proceed. The man answered: You have only to walk about until your legs are heavy, and then to lie down, and the poison will act. At the same time he handed the cup to Socrates, who in the easiest and gentlest manner, without the least fear or change of colour or feature, looking at the man with all his eyes, Echecrates, as his manner was, took the cup and said: What do you say about making a libation out of this cup to any god? May I, or not? The man answered: We only prepare, Socrates, just so much as we deem enough. I understand, he said: but I may and must ask the gods to prosper my journey from this to the other world--even so--and so be it according to my prayer. Then raising the cup to his lips, quite readily and cheerfully he drank off the poison. And hitherto most of us had been able to control our sorrow; but now when we saw him drinking, and saw too that he had finished the draught, we could no longer forbear, and in spite of myself my own tears were flowing fast; so that I covered my face and wept, not for him, but at the thought of my own calamity in having to part from such a friend. Nor was I the first; for Crito, when he found himself unable to restrain his tears, had got up, and I followed; and at that moment, Apollodorus, who had been weeping all the time, broke out in a loud and passionate cry which made cowards of us all. Socrates alone retained his calmness: What is this strange outcry? he said. I sent away the women mainly in order that they might not misbehave in this way, for I have been told that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, then, and have patience. When we heard his words we were ashamed, and refrained our tears; and he walked about until, as he said, his legs began to fail, and then he lay on his back, according to the directions, and the man who gave him the poison now and then looked at his feet and legs; and after a while he pressed his foot hard, and asked him if he could feel; and he said, No; and then his leg, and so upwards and upwards, and showed us that he was cold and stiff. And he felt them himself, and said: When the poison reaches the heart, that will be the end. He was beginning to grow cold about the groin, when he uncovered his face, for he had covered himself up, and said--they were his last words--he said: Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt? The debt shall be paid, said Crito; is there anything else? There was no answer to this question; but in a minute or two a movement was heard, and the attendants uncovered him; his eyes were set, and Crito closed his eyes and mouth.
Such was the end, Echecrates, of our friend; concerning whom I may truly say, that of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.

ap1.essay:
The title misleads in English. An apologia is a defence speech; nobody here says sorry for anything. And the first thing Socrates does is tell five hundred or so jurors that he cannot make speeches, in a paragraph that is a very well made speech. Disclaiming eloquence was a stock courtroom opening in Athens, and I think the jury would have heard it as one. What is unusual is that he then means it. He asks to be treated as 'a stranger' talking in his native tongue, the talk of 'the agora, at the tables of the money-changers', and for the rest of the day that is what they get: questions, homely comparisons, no appeal for pity. Whether that was wise is the question the whole Apology leaves open.

Then comes the move I admire most as tactics and trust least as law. He sets the actual indictment aside and announces that his real prosecutors are not in court. For decades people have talked of 'one Socrates, a wise man' who pries into the sky and under the earth and 'made the worse appear the better cause'. That is two slanders rolled together, the natural scientist who explains the gods away and the sophist who sells clever speaking, and neither is what he does. But the jurors took them in as children, a rumour cannot be cross-examined, and the only name he can attach is 'a Comic poet'. Aristophanes put a Socrates on stage in the Clouds in 423, hung up in a basket and announcing that he 'walks in air'. Twenty-four years of a joke is a kind of evidence.

His answers are brisk. On science he simply asks the jurors to tell each other whether any of them ever heard him discuss it. (The Phaedo has him admit to a youthful passion for exactly this; see [[phb1]].) On teaching for pay he is funnier: Gorgias, Prodicus, Hippias, and now Evenus at five minæ a course, with Socrates congratulating him 'if he really has this wisdom'. The little scene with Callias about foals and calves holds most of his philosophy. We know whom to hire to make a horse a good horse. Whom do we hire to make a son a good man? It sounds like a joke about school fees, but he is asking whether such knowledge exists at all, and that question is the plot of the [[me1|Meno]].

What strikes me on rereading is how little of this is defence. He is denying rumours no one has formally charged him with, and clearing the ground for a story.

annotations.quote: unless by the force of eloquence they mean the force of truth
annotations.note: A neat rhetorical turn in the middle of a claim to have no rhetoric. I don't think it is hypocrisy. He is redefining the word in front of them, which is what he does to words all day long.

annotations.quote: I would have you regard me as if I were really a stranger
annotations.note: Seventy years old and never once in a law court, in the most litigious city in Greece. He asks for the allowance one makes for a foreigner's accent. It is an odd thing to feel foreign in the courts of the only city you have ever lived in, and I think he means the oddness.

annotations.quote: let the speaker speak truly and the judge decide justly
annotations.note: A division of labour he will hold them to. Later he refuses to beg for mercy on exactly this ground: the juror's job is to judge, not to be moved. Notice too that he addresses them as 'men of Athens' and never as judges, and watch when that finally changes in [[ap7]].

annotations.quote: and I am more afraid of them than of Anytus and his associates
annotations.note: Anytus, a prominent democratic politician, is the weight behind the prosecution; Meletus merely signed it. Socrates names the powerful man first and then says he is the lesser danger. The jury's own childhood memories worry him more.

annotations.quote: I must simply fight with shadows in my own defence
annotations.note: The predicament of anyone with a reputation. You can cross-examine a prosecutor, and he will, with relish, in [[ap3]]. You cannot cross-examine what everybody has always heard.

annotations.quote: unless in the chance case of a Comic poet
annotations.note: Aristophanes, named outright two paragraphs on. The Clouds showed a Socrates who ran a school, studied gnats and the heavens, and taught young men to argue their way out of debts. Many jurors would have seen it, or grown up on its jokes.

annotations.quote: And so leaving the event with God, in obedience to the law I will now make my defence.
annotations.note: 'Event' in the old sense of outcome. The sentence names his two authorities side by side, the god and the law, and the rest of the speech, and the Crito after it, is about what happens when they pull apart.

annotations.quote: if your two sons were foals or calves, there would be no difficulty in finding some one to put over them
annotations.note: The trainer comparison is his favourite tool and it comes back against Meletus. Behind it is a real claim: being a good human being might be a skill with experts, like horse-breeding. If so, who are they? Callias, who had spent more on sophists than anyone in Athens, is the right man to ask.

annotations.quote: Happy is Evenus, I said to myself, if he really has this wisdom, and teaches at such a moderate charge.
annotations.note: Five minæ was a great deal of money, so 'moderate' is dry. Keep the figure in mind. When Socrates has to put a price on his own life in [[ap6]], his first offer is one.

links.why: The Euthyphro opens on the porch of the court a few weeks earlier, with Socrates explaining who Meletus is and what the indictment says.
The question put to Callias, whether anyone can teach human excellence, is the opening question of the Meno, and Anytus turns up there in person.
In prison Socrates tells how, as a young man, he was in fact fascinated by natural science and by Anaxagoras, which complicates the flat denial here.
The horse-trainer comparison returns as a weapon in the cross-examination of Meletus.

ap2.essay:
Here is the story everything else depends on, and Socrates knows how it will sound: he warns the jury twice not to shout him down before he gets it out. A friend of his, the impetuous Chaerephon, went to Delphi and asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the priestess said that no one was. Look at the form of that answer. It is not 'Socrates is the wisest of men', which is how Socrates himself paraphrases it a few lines later. It is that nobody is wiser, which could be true of a world in which nobody is wise at all. That turns out to be more or less his conclusion.

What he does next is the thing I find most characteristic of him. He is sure of two things that cannot both be true: he has 'no wisdom, small or great', and the god 'cannot lie'. A pious man would accept the oracle and a sceptic would shrug it off. Socrates treats it as a riddle and tests it by trying to prove it wrong. He will find one wiser man and take him to Delphi 'with a refutation in my hand'. I love the cheek of that. His obedience to the god takes the form of cross-examining the god. And the method he invents for the purpose, going to someone with a reputation and asking questions until the reputation gives way, is the method of every other dialogue in this book. The [[eu1|Euthyphro]] is one of these interviews at full length: a man quite sure he knows what piety is, until he is asked.

The three rounds are worth keeping apart, because the three groups fail differently. The politicians have nothing; the first of them is 'thought wise by many, and still wiser by himself', a clause Jowett must have enjoyed writing. The poets have something real, but it is not knowledge. They write 'by a sort of genius and inspiration' and cannot explain their own best passages, which any bystander could discuss better. (I think this is unfair to poets, and also true of a good many.) The artisans are the interesting case. They do know things, Socrates says so plainly, and 'in this they certainly were wiser than I was.' Their mistake is to suppose that being good at a trade qualifies them on 'all sorts of high matters'. Of the three diagnoses it is the one that has aged least. We still ask the surgeon about politics and the millionaire about schools.

Out of this comes the famous formula, and it is more modest than its reputation. He does not say 'I know that I know nothing', which would be a boast and a contradiction at once. He says of the politician, 'he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know', and claims to have 'slightly the advantage'. Slightly. The wisdom consists in lacking one particular error. Then he reads the oracle as hardly about himself at all. The god is 'only using my name by way of illustration', as one might say 'take Socrates, for instance'. Human wisdom is 'worth little or nothing', and the wisest person is whoever has noticed.

Is the humility real? I go back and forth. A man who calls his errand 'Herculean' labours and himself the god's chosen example is not short of self-regard, and the jury evidently heard arrogance; that is why he has to keep asking for quiet. But I don't think it is a pose. The claim is narrow and he keeps to it all day. When he comes to death, in [[ap4]], he applies the same test and declines to say he knows it is bad.

Two practical things are also being done. The story explains the hatred without any wrongdoing on his part: every examination was held in public, each one made 'another enemy', and the rich young men who trailed after him went home and tried it on their elders. The stock charges, sky and earth and no gods, are what people reach for when someone asks what exactly he teaches and they 'do not know, and cannot tell'. And the story converts a habit into a duty. By the end he is 'obedient to the god', in 'utter poverty by reason of my devotion', and his three accusers are merely delegates of the professions he embarrassed: Meletus for the poets, Anytus for the craftsmen and politicians, Lycon for the orators. A man on trial for impiety has just described his whole life as a religious mission. That is either the best defence available or a fresh provocation, and I suspect it was both.

A word on Jowett's 'God'. The Greek says 'the god', meaning Apollo of Delphi. The capital letter and the churchly cadence make Socrates sound closer to a Christian than he was; 'necessity was laid upon me' is very nearly St Paul. Keep the whole of Olympus in mind when he says it.

annotations.quote: there must have been something strange which you have been doing
annotations.note: He hands the jury its own best objection, no smoke without fire, and calls it 'a fair challenge'. He agrees there was something strange. The rest of the section is his account of what it was.

annotations.quote: for he shared in the recent exile of the people, and returned with you
annotations.note: A political credential slipped in sideways. Chaerephon went into exile with the democrats when the Thirty seized Athens in 404 and came back with them. Socrates stayed in the city. Reminding a democratic jury that his oldest friend was one of them is not accidental.

annotations.quote: then I might go to the god with a refutation in my hand
annotations.note: The mission begins as an attempt to catch Apollo out. It is a strange kind of reverence, and one worth remembering in a trial for irreverence: he takes the oracle seriously enough to argue with it.

annotations.quote: for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know
annotations.note: The original of the saying usually misquoted as 'I know that I know nothing'. What he claims is smaller: he lacks the false belief. Note too what the ignorance is about, 'anything really beautiful and good'. He is talking about how to live. He never doubts that shoemakers know shoes.

annotations.quote: by the dog I swear!—for I must tell you the truth
annotations.note: His private oath, used in other dialogues too, and nobody is quite sure where he got it. To a jury deciding whether he respects the city's gods, swearing by a dog in the middle of a story about Apollo cannot have helped. He does it anyway.

annotations.quote: not by wisdom do poets write poetry, but by a sort of genius and inspiration
annotations.note: Plato will return to this idea for the rest of his career. It is half a compliment: the poems really are fine, and something really does speak through the poet. The complaint is that the poet takes the credit and then extends it to subjects he knows nothing about.

annotations.quote: because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters
annotations.note: The sharpest observation in the section, I think. Real competence in one field produces confidence in every field. It is also aimed at the jury: Athenian democracy ran on the assumption that any competent citizen could judge the highest matters.

annotations.quote: he is only using my name by way of illustration
annotations.note: The compliment from Delphi shrinks to a grammatical example. I find this both graceful and a little sly, since the conclusion still leaves him, of all men in Athens, the one the god picked.

annotations.quote: This confounded Socrates, they say; this villainous misleader of youth!
annotations.note: Jowett's stage Victorian, which I enjoy. The mechanism matters more than the diction: the corruption charge comes from fathers who were shown up by their own sons using his method. The sons are imitating him without his permission, and he gets the blame.

links.why: A complete specimen of the kind of examination described here: a self-declared expert on piety, met on the way to this very trial.
The Meno opens with another confident man asked to say what he is so sure he knows.
The test invented here, do you actually know that, is applied to the fear of death.
His picture of the afterlife is this section over again: going from one famous person to the next, finding out who is wise.

ap3.essay:
This is the only stretch of the Apology that is a dialogue, and it is the least loved. Athenian procedure let a defendant question his accuser, who was obliged to answer, and Socrates uses the right to do to Meletus in ten minutes what he has spent a lifetime doing to other people. I'll admit it makes me slightly uneasy. It is very funny, and it is not quite fair.

The first trap is about who improves the young. Meletus, who has plainly never considered the matter, says the laws, then the jurors, the audience, the Council (Jowett's 'senators'), the Assembly: everyone in Athens but one man. Then the horses come back from the talk with Callias in [[ap1]]. With horses, a few trainers improve them and most people who handle them do harm. It is a good point against Meletus and an awkward one to make to a democratic jury, since it implies that most of them are no use to their own sons. Anytus, sitting with the prosecution, has this exact quarrel with Socrates in the [[me1|Meno]], and ends it with a threat.

The second trap is Socratic doctrine in legal dress. No one wants to live among bad neighbours, so no one would knowingly make his neighbours bad, so if he corrupts anyone it is by mistake, and a mistake calls for teaching. He describes a law court as 'a place not of instruction, but of punishment', and the complaint goes deeper than it looks. He thinks all wrongdoing is a kind of ignorance, which, taken seriously, would put the courts out of business.

Then the religious charge, and here I think Meletus loses the argument unaided. Asked whether he means strange gods or no gods, he reaches for the bigger claim: 'a complete atheist.' That lets Socrates pin him with his own indictment, which speaks of 'new divinities'. Spiritual things imply spirits; spirits are gods or the children of gods; you might as well believe in mules and deny horses and asses. As logic it is tidy. As an answer it slides past what the charge was really about, whether he honours the city's gods in the city's way. He never says the plain sentence a nervous juror wanted to hear, and Euthyphro's guess in [[eu1]], that the real trouble is his private divine sign, goes unaddressed until [[ap5]].

So Meletus is shown to be careless, which is all Socrates promised to prove. Whether showing up your prosecutor wins over a jury is another matter. Each of them has just watched, live, the thing his enemies had been describing.

annotations.quote: that good man and true lover of his country, as he calls himself
annotations.note: The sarcasm arrives before the first question. In the Euthyphro Socrates describes Meletus as a young unknown with a beak of a nose and a thin beard, and the tone is the same: elaborate politeness about a man he cannot take seriously.

annotations.quote: Observe, Meletus, that you are silent, and have nothing to say.
annotations.note: Plato writes the pause into the speech. Socrates narrates his opponent's silence to the jury as a piece of evidence, which is a cross-examiner's trick and a rather ruthless one.

annotations.quote: Then every Athenian improves and elevates them; all with the exception of myself
annotations.note: Meletus has been flattering his way up through every body of citizens present and finds he has walked into an absurdity. He 'stoutly' affirms it anyway. He cannot back down now without insulting someone in the room.

annotations.quote: Does one man do them harm and all the world good?
annotations.note: The argument from expertise again. I think it is right about horses and risky about citizens. A democracy assumes that bringing up the young is everybody's business, and the trainer comparison denies that outright.

annotations.quote: And now you bring me up in this court, which is a place not of instruction, but of punishment.
annotations.note: A reproach I find oddly sincere under the irony. If Meletus truly believed Socrates was doing harm, the decent course was to come and tell him. Nobody ever did; they went to law after decades of silence.

annotations.quote: I mean the latter—that you are a complete atheist.
annotations.note: The overreach that undoes him. The indictment charged new divinities, which was at least arguable. By upgrading it to no gods at all, Meletus contradicts his own document and gives Socrates an easy target in place of a hard one.

annotations.quote: Friend Meletus, you think that you are accusing Anaxagoras
annotations.note: Anaxagoras of Clazomenae taught in Athens a generation earlier that the sun was a glowing stone, and is said to have been prosecuted for impiety himself. Meletus has reached for the old Clouds caricature, exactly as [[ap1]] predicted his kind would.

annotations.quote: and they might pay their money, and laugh at Socrates if he pretends to father these extraordinary views
annotations.note: The young could pick these ideas up for a drachma, he says, so who would need him? A good joke that also makes a quiet point: Athens tolerated these doctrines when they came in a book or a play. Something else about him is the offence.

annotations.quote: You might as well affirm the existence of mules, and deny that of horses and asses.
annotations.note: The earthiest line in the argument, and the stable again; he can hardly get through a paragraph without livestock. Jowett's 'demigods' and 'spiritual agencies' translate one family of Greek words, daimones and daimonia, and the whole proof is a play on their kinship.

links.why: Socrates' first description of Meletus and of the charge, and Euthyphro's guess about what lies behind it.
The Meno asks in earnest the question Meletus fumbles here: who, if anyone, makes the young better?
The foals and calves of the talk with Callias are the model for the horse-trainer argument used here.
The divine sign, the real substance of the 'new divinities' charge, is finally explained there.

ap4.essay:
With Meletus disposed of, Socrates says the indictment was never the danger, and turns to a question a kinder listener might put: aren't you ashamed to have lived in a way that has brought you to this? What follows is the centre of the speech. It is hardly a defence any more. It reads more like a statement of terms.

He starts by reaching, of all people, for Achilles. The 'son of Thetis' was told by his mother that killing Hector would cost him his own life, and chose it rather than sit by the ships 'a laughing-stock and a burden of the earth'. A snub-nosed man of seventy, a foot soldier in his day, is setting himself beside the greatest warrior in Homer, and I think he means the jury to feel the stretch. What he keeps from Achilles is the rule: a man 'ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying', only whether he is doing right. What he changes is everything else. Achilles stays for revenge and glory. Socrates stays to ask people questions. Then he brings it down to earth with his own campaigns, Potidaea, Amphipolis and Delium, where he stood where the generals put him. If he held his post for them, he can hardly desert the one the god assigned.

The argument about death is the oracle story of [[ap2]] applied to the hardest case. To fear death is to claim to know that it is bad, and nobody knows that; it might be 'the greatest good'. So the fear is one more instance of 'the conceit that a man knows what he does not know'. I find this bracing and not wholly convincing. One can fear a thing precisely because it is unknown. But see how he balances it. Against the unknown he sets one thing he says he does know, that 'injustice and disobedience to a better' is evil. The man who knows nothing knows that. He will not avoid 'a possible good rather than a certain evil'. Everything he does from here on, the refusal to beg in [[ap5]], the refusal of exile in [[ap6]], the refusal to escape in the [[cr1|Crito]], is that sentence acted on.

Then he makes the jury an offer on their own behalf and turns it down. Suppose you let me go on condition that I stop. 'Men of Athens, I honour and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you.' The English has the ring of the Acts of the Apostles and Jowett surely meant it to, but the thought needed no help. A defendant is telling a court beforehand that he will ignore its order. It is worth setting this beside the Crito, where the same man argues that he must not break the city's laws even to save his life. People have argued for a long time over whether the two fit together. I think they do. He will not obey a command to do wrong, and he will not run from the penalty for refusing. He disobeys in the open and stays for the consequences.

What he would go on saying is given word for word, and it is the plainest summary of his teaching anywhere in Plato: you belong to a great city; are you not ashamed to care so much for 'money and honour and reputation' and so little for 'the greatest improvement of the soul'? There is no doctrine here about what a soul is, and no theory. There is an order of priorities, pressed on one person at a time, with a follow-up question for anyone who says he already cares.

The last two paragraphs raise the stakes in a way that must have been hard to sit through. You cannot hurt me, he says: 'a bad man is not permitted to injure a better than himself.' Kill, exile, disfranchise, yes, but those are not injuries; the injury falls on whoever does the injustice. So he is pleading for their sake and not his own. And then the image everyone remembers, which he himself calls 'ludicrous': Athens is a big well-bred horse gone sluggish, and he is the gadfly the god has fastened on it. It is a wonderful piece of self-description because it concedes the prosecution's whole experience of him. He is irritating. He bites. The sleeper's first impulse is to slap. His only claim is that the city needs waking, and his only evidence that he means it is that he never took a fee.

Is this arrogance? Xenophon, who also wrote up the trial, thought Socrates talked so loftily that he must have decided he was better off dead. I read it differently. He has settled what he is, and he declines to pretend otherwise for one afternoon.

annotations.quote: not Meletus, nor yet Anytus, but the envy and detraction of the world
annotations.note: He predicts the verdict in the middle of his defence and names the cause as something no speech can answer. The aside that he won't be the last good man to die this way is as near to bitterness as he gets.

annotations.quote: a laughing-stock and a burden of the earth
annotations.note: Achilles in the Iliad, quoted loosely from memory. For a Homeric hero the worst fate is to be useless and laughed at. Socrates borrows the feeling and changes its object: the disgrace he fears is abandoning philosophy, something no one in Homer would have recognised as a post.

annotations.quote: For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom
annotations.note: The boldest use of his one principle. Everyone in court assumes death is the worst thing that can happen; that assumption is what gives the prosecution its power over him. He removes it by asking how they know.

annotations.quote: Men of Athens, I honour and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you
annotations.note: The affection is meant, I think, and so is the refusal. The Greek has 'the god', Apollo; Jowett's wording puts the apostles' answer to the Sanhedrin into his mouth. Read this against the [[cr1|Crito]], where he will not disobey the city even to live.

annotations.quote: are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation
annotations.note: This is the corrupting doctrine, quoted in full by the accused. Shame is the lever every time. He was just asked whether he is ashamed of his life, and here he hands the word back to the whole city.

annotations.quote: not even if I have to die many times
annotations.note: At this point he has stopped trying to be acquitted, if he ever was trying. A defendant who tells the jury that no verdict will change his behaviour has left them one way to stop him.

annotations.quote: for a bad man is not permitted to injure a better than himself
annotations.note: 'Not permitted' by the order of things, by the gods. The only real harm is becoming worse, and nobody can do that to you but you. It is his hardest saying and he restates it at the very end as 'no evil can happen to a good man'. I am not sure I believe it. He clearly does.

annotations.quote: am a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God
annotations.note: The comparison is his own and he apologises for it as he makes it. What I like is that it flatters nobody: the city is a fine horse half asleep, and he is an insect. A man angling for sympathy would have picked a different animal.

annotations.quote: And I have a sufficient witness to the truth of what I say—my poverty.
annotations.note: The dash is perfectly timed. Every other witness in the speech is a person or a god; this one is a condition. It answers the sophist charge of [[ap1]] better than any denial, since nobody stays poor for forty years as a business plan.

links.why: The necessary companion: the man who here says he will disobey the court argues there that he must not disobey the laws.
The oracle story supplies both the 'post' he will not desert and the test he applies to the fear of death.
On his last day he goes further than 'no one knows' and gives his friends reasons for hoping that death is good.
The principle of never choosing a certain evil over a possible good decides the question of the counter-penalty.

ap5.essay:
An obvious question hangs over the gadfly: if he cares so much about Athens, why did he never speak in the Assembly? The answer brings in the oddest fact about him, the 'sign', a 'kind of voice' he has heard since childhood. Its rule is strict: 'it always forbids but never commands.' It never tells him what to do or what is true. It only stops him. This is what Meletus's indictment turned into 'new divinities', and Socrates mentions the connection almost in passing, as if it were not the heart of the religious charge.

What the sign kept him out of was politics, and his gloss on that is the bleakest sentence in the speech: no one who honestly opposes 'you or any other multitude' will survive, so a man who means to fight for the right 'must have a private station'. He gives two stories, carefully paired. Under the democracy, in 406, serving on the Council's presiding committee, he alone opposed the illegal mass trial of the generals after Arginusae, with the Assembly howling at him. Under the Thirty, the junta of 404, he was ordered with four others to fetch Leon of Salamis for execution. One regime of each kind, and the same answer to both. I think the pairing is aimed at a charge nobody could make aloud, that he had been the teacher of oligarchs. Critias, who led the Thirty, and Alcibiades had both kept his company, and the amnesty of 403 made that awkward to put in an indictment. 'Those who are slanderously termed my disciples' is as near as he comes.

I will say what bothers me about 'I went quietly home'. Leon died. Socrates refused to do the wrong and did nothing to prevent it. That is the limit of a private station, and he does not hide it.

The roll-call moves me more than the arguments do. If he ruined the young, where are the ruined, or their fathers and brothers? He points around the court: Crito and his son, the father of Aeschines, and 'Adeimantus the son of Ariston, whose brother Plato is present'. The author signs his work here, as a witness.

Last comes the refusal that probably cost him the verdict. Defendants were expected to produce weeping children. He has three sons and will not bring them, because a juror has sworn to judge by the laws and not to 'make a present of justice'; to beg him to break that oath would be teaching impiety at a trial for impiety. It is rigorous, and to anyone who had once wept in that court himself it was an insult. He seems to know.

annotations.quote: it always forbids but never commands me to do anything which I am going to do
annotations.note: The famous daimonion, and it is a much smaller thing than a guardian spirit. It gives no advice and reveals nothing. It is a brake. Everything positive in his life he has to reason out for himself, which is why he can honour the sign and still argue about everything.

annotations.quote: must have a private station and not a public one
annotations.note: A hard verdict on Athenian democracy, delivered to five hundred of its citizens. He is not saying politics is beneath him. He is saying an honest man in it gets killed, and the day's proceedings are about to supply the example.

annotations.quote: I was the only one of the Prytanes who was opposed to the illegality
annotations.note: The Prytanes were the fifty Council members, one tribe at a time, who presided for a tenth of the year; Jowett's 'senator' is a councillor chosen by lot. So in his single turn at ordinary civic duty Socrates ended up alone against the Assembly, on a point of law. The jury 'all thought afterwards' that he was right.

annotations.quote: the other four went to Salamis and fetched Leon, but I went quietly home
annotations.note: The 'rotunda' is the round building where the Council's committee met, taken over by the Thirty. I admire the flatness of this. No speech, no defiance, he just goes home. It is also the sentence in the Apology I find hardest to be comfortable with, because the other four did go.

annotations.quote: Not that I have any regular disciples.
annotations.note: The denial covers real ground. He took no fees and ran no school, so no one could be his pupil in the sense that Evenus had pupils. But Critias and Alcibiades sat at his elbow for years, everyone in court knew it, and neither name is spoken.

annotations.quote: and Adeimantus the son of Ariston, whose brother Plato is present
annotations.note: Plato names himself only three times in all his dialogues: twice in this speech, as present, and once in the Phaedo, as absent through illness. Here it works as a claim on the reader's trust. I was there, he is telling us, and my family would have testified.

annotations.quote: I have a family, yes, and sons, O Athenians, three in number, one almost a man, and two others who are still young
annotations.note: The one glimpse of his household, and he gives it only to explain why he will not use it. Two small boys and a father of seventy. He returns to these sons in the last lines of the speech, with a request nobody would expect.

annotations.quote: For his duty is, not to make a present of justice, but to give judgment
annotations.note: Jowett's 'judge' is a juror, one of hundreds of ordinary citizens with no presiding magistrate to instruct them. Socrates gives them the instruction himself: a verdict is not theirs to hand out as a favour. He is right, and he is lecturing the people about to vote on him.

annotations.quote: and in a sense higher than that in which any of my accusers believe in them
annotations.note: At last the direct statement that the cross-examination of Meletus withheld, and even now it has an edge. He does believe in gods, but in 'a sense higher' than his accusers do. He cannot affirm his orthodoxy without implying theirs is the shallower kind.

links.why: Euthyphro guesses at once that the sign is what the 'new gods' charge is really about.
Crito, pointed out here in court, is the friend who comes to the prison before dawn with an escape plan.
Several of the men named in this roll-call are at the deathbed, and there Plato records his own absence.
The two stories are offered as proof in deeds of the claim made there, that he would not do wrong to avoid death.

ap6.essay:
Between the last section and this one the jury has voted, and he has lost by less than he expected. Thirty votes the other way would have acquitted him, on a jury of five hundred something like 280 to 220. In a case of this kind the law fixed no penalty. The prosecutor proposed one, the convicted man proposed another, and the jury had to choose between the two with no power to split the difference. Meletus asks for death. Everything in the system invites Socrates to name something severe enough to be accepted, and everyone in court knows the word is exile.

What he proposes is dinner. Reasoning aloud from the question 'what is my due?', he arrives at free meals for life in the Prytaneum, the public hall where Athens fed its Olympic victors and benefactors. His comparison with the winning charioteer is sharp: the victor 'only gives you the appearance of happiness, and I give you the reality.' I have never been able to decide how to take this. It is a joke, and it is also the strict consequence of what he has said all day. If the mission is a service to the city, then naming a punishment would be a lie, and he says so: 'I will not say of myself that I deserve any evil.' The joke and the principle are the same thing here, and it was the joke the jury could not forgive.

Then he runs through the real options, and each one fails by the logic of [[ap4]]. Death he does not know to be bad. Prison, a fine he cannot pay, and exile he does know to be bad. The exile passage is the saddest thing in the speech: an old man 'wandering from city to city', gathering young listeners and being moved on by their fathers. In the [[cr1|Crito]] the Laws of Athens will remind him that he could have had exile with the city's consent at this moment and chose otherwise.

When an imagined voice suggests that he simply keep quiet abroad, he gives the line that has outlived everything else he said: 'the unexamined life is not worth living.' Read it where it sits. It is not offered as a motto. It comes inside a sentence about how he expects to be disbelieved. He has two explanations of why he cannot stop, the god's command and this one, and he says the jury will find the second harder to credit than the first.

The ending is close to comedy. He could manage one mina. Then his friends prompt him and it becomes thirty, with Plato among the guarantors. I think it came too late.

annotations.quote: had thirty votes gone over to the other side, I should have been acquitted
annotations.note: A tie counted as acquittal, so thirty changed votes would have done it. He is 'only surprised' the margin is so thin, which tells you he never expected to win. Note for later that the jury was this close before he opened his mouth again.

annotations.quote: And I may say, I think, that I have escaped Meletus.
annotations.note: A joke in arithmetic. Three accusers, so credit each with a third of the guilty votes, and Meletus on his own falls short of the fifth of the jury a prosecutor needed to avoid a fine for a frivolous suit. He has just been convicted and he is doing sums at Meletus's expense.

annotations.quote: the man who has never had the wit to be idle during his whole life
annotations.note: Jowett's 'wit' here means sense: he never had the good sense to keep quiet. Socrates describes forty years of philosophy the way an exasperated relative might, and then lists everything he neglected for it, which is everything an Athenian gentleman cared about.

annotations.quote: There can be no reward so fitting as maintenance in the Prytaneum
annotations.note: The sacred hearth of the city, where honoured guests and victorious athletes dined at public cost. Asked to name his punishment, he names the highest civic honour Athens had. I can't read it without imagining the noise in the court.

annotations.quote: that a capital cause should not be decided in one day
annotations.note: A reasonable complaint tucked inside the provocation. Sparta, for one, took longer over capital cases. Athenian trials ran by the water-clock and ended by nightfall, and his whole method depends on having time to go slowly with one person.

annotations.quote: When I do not know whether death is a good or an evil, why should I propose a penalty which would certainly be an evil?
annotations.note: The argument of [[ap4]] put to practical use, and it has a consequence he must see: by this reasoning death is the only sentence he has no grounds to refuse. He is arguing himself toward Meletus's proposal.

annotations.quote: And what a life should I lead, at my age, wandering from city to city
annotations.note: For once he sounds tired. He knows exactly how it would go, because it is how it went at home. Either he sends the young men away and they complain, or he lets them stay and their fathers complain. There is no city where the questioning is welcome.

annotations.quote: and that the unexamined life is not worth living, you are still less likely to believe me
annotations.note: The most quoted sentence in philosophy, and he delivers it as something he knows will not land. Notice also what he calls the greatest good just before: 'daily to discourse about virtue'. He means talking, with other people, every day. He is not recommending solitary self-scrutiny.

annotations.quote: Well, perhaps I could afford a mina, and therefore I propose that penalty
annotations.note: A mina was a hundred drachmas, a few months' pay for a craftsman. Evenus in [[ap1]] charged five for his course. So Socrates prices his life at a fifth of a sophist's fee, and means it; it is what he has.

links.why: The Laws throw this moment back at him: he could have proposed exile at the trial and declared he preferred death.
Every option is weighed by the rule laid down there, never to choose a known evil over a possible good.
Evenus and his five minæ, for comparison with the one mina offered here.

ap7.essay:
The jury has chosen death, and a later tradition says by a wider margin than it had found him guilty, which after the Prytaneum I can believe. What Plato gives him now is not strictly part of a trial. Whether a condemned man was really allowed to go on talking, nobody knows. These last pages read to me like Plato's own leave-taking, and they are divided between two audiences.

To those who voted for death he is cold. They have gained very little time, since he is old and would soon have died anyway. He was convicted, he says, because he would not grovel, and he would make the same choice again. Then comes the image of the two runners. Death is slow and has caught an old man; wickedness is quicker and has caught his accusers. And he prophesies that more critics will come, younger and harsher, whom he has so far held back. The book in our hands was written by one of them, so the prophecy was at least partly kept.

Then the tone changes entirely. He turns to those who voted to acquit, asks them to stay 'while the magistrates are busy', and for the first time all day calls his hearers 'judges', remarking that these have earned the word. To them he offers a private piece of evidence, the silence of the sign. It stopped him over trifles all his life, and today it let him leave the house, enter the court, and say every provoking thing he said. So what has happened must be good. I find this touching and, as reasoning, a little dizzying: the divine voice the city is killing him for is produced as proof that being killed is all right.

The argument that follows is deliberately modest. Death is either a dreamless sleep or a journey to another place. If it is sleep, then 'to die is gain', Jowett lending him St Paul's phrase, since even the king of Persia has had few nights better than a dreamless one. If it is a journey, he will find real judges, and Homer, and men like Palamedes and Ajax who were also wrongly condemned, and he will go on doing exactly what he did in Athens. That is his heaven: more conversation. He does not pretend to know which it will be. The [[pha1|Phaedo]] has him argue hard on his last day that the soul survives; here he is still the man of [[ap2]], who will not claim what he does not know.

His last request is that his sons be pestered as he pestered Athens. And the last sentence settles nothing, which I think is why it has lasted.

annotations.quote: I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live
annotations.note: This answers the opening request in [[ap1]], where he asked leave to talk as he always talks. He sees how he spoke and whether he lived as a single matter. A speech that saved him by flattery would have been made by someone else.

annotations.quote: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.
annotations.note: A footrace with two pursuers. Old and slow, he has been caught by the slower one; his accusers, 'keen and quick', by the faster. It is the neatest image in the speech and carries his claim from [[ap4]] that doing wrong is worse than suffering it.

annotations.quote: accusers whom hitherto I have restrained
annotations.note: A startling thing to learn at this stage: he regards himself as having been the moderate one. The young men who copied his questioning were held in check by his presence. With him gone they will be angrier and less polite, and at least one of them will write it all down.

annotations.quote: O my judges—for you I may truly call judges
annotations.note: All day he has said 'men of Athens' or 'Athenians'. The title is granted only now, and only to the minority who voted to acquit, on the ground that a judge is someone who judges justly. It is a small, exact piece of bookkeeping carried through the entire speech.

annotations.quote: But the oracle made no sign of opposition
annotations.note: Jowett uses 'oracle' here for the inner sign, the same word he used for Delphi, which blurs two different things in the Greek. The reasoning from silence is the only time in the Apology that the sign is treated as telling him something, and it tells him by not speaking.

annotations.quote: for eternity is then only a single night
annotations.note: The most beautiful sentence in the speech, I think, and the least argued. A cool head would object that a night of dreamless sleep is pleasant only because one wakes and notices. He does not stop for that, and at this hour I would not ask him to.

annotations.quote: In another world they do not put a man to death for asking questions: assuredly not.
annotations.note: The one joke aimed at the verdict, and it is gentle. Look at whom he wants to examine down there: Agamemnon, Sisyphus, Odysseus, the very man who got Palamedes killed and beat Ajax to the arms of Achilles. Even among the dead he plans to cross-examine the clever ones.

annotations.quote: I would have you trouble them, as I have troubled you
annotations.note: He asks the city that condemned him to be a gadfly to his children. The request is wry, and it is also the highest compliment he can pay his own way of life: it is what he wants for the people he loves. 'Punish' in the same sentence means only this.

annotations.quote: Which is better God only knows.
annotations.note: After an hour of arguing that death may be a good, he ends by not knowing. The last word is the ignorance he started with in the oracle story. Jowett's capital G again covers a Greek phrase that says only 'the god'.

links.why: The promised death, a month later, with a far more confident account of what the soul can hope for.
The next scene in the story: the prison, the wait for the ship from Delos, and Crito's offer of escape.
The afterlife he imagines is the Delphic mission continued, and the final sentence returns to its confession of ignorance.
For the other end of the journey sketched here: the myth of the world below and the death scene itself.

cr1.essay:
The Crito is the shortest thing in this book and the only one with nobody watching. The [[ap1|Apology]] was a speech to some five hundred jurors; this is two old men in a cell before sunrise, about a month after the verdict, and one of them has been sitting in the dark watching the other sleep. I find that opening image hard to get past. Crito has come to say that the ship is nearly in and the time nearly gone, and he cannot bring himself to wake the man he has come to save. Socrates' 'peaceful slumbers' are already the answer to everything Crito is about to say. The rest of the dialogue only spells it out.

What I notice most in this first stretch is how badly Crito argues and how much I like him for it. He is rich, loyal, practical and frightened, and his reasons come tumbling out in the order he feels them, not in the order of their strength. First: what will people think of me? Then: never mind the cost, the informers come cheap. Then: I have friends in Thessaly. Only then the two that actually bite: you are doing your enemies' work for them, and you are abandoning your sons. By the end he is accusing a man who has accepted death of choosing 'the easier part', and announcing that 'the time of deliberation is over', which may be the least Socratic sentence anyone speaks in Plato.

It would be easy to take Crito as a foil, the ordinary man who does not get it. I don't think Plato wants that. The point about the children is never really answered anywhere in the dialogue; it is only outweighed. And Crito's shame is well founded: he will in fact be thought a man who kept his money and lost his friend. What Plato shows is a decent person reasoning from love and reputation, which is how most of us reason most of the time, and then he asks whether that is good enough when the stakes are highest.

Socrates' replies here are short and almost offhand. The many cannot do the greatest harm, he says, because they cannot make anyone wise or foolish. It sounds like a paradox thrown out to change the subject. It is the whole argument in miniature, and [[cr2|the next section]] unpacks it. Notice the dream, too. Before a single reason has been given, a woman in bright raiment has already told him he is going home.

annotations.quote: I have done him a kindness
annotations.note: Jowett's tactful phrase for what is presumably a tip to the jailer. It tells you at once what kind of man Crito is: someone who gets things done through favours and money, and who has already been quietly using both. The escape he is about to propose would run on the same fuel.

annotations.quote: I have been watching with amazement your peaceful slumbers
annotations.note: The visitor is the one in distress and the condemned man is the one asleep. Crito says he held off 'to minimize the pain', but the pain is his own. Plato sets the two tempers side by side before either has argued anything.

annotations.quote: as persons who have come from Sunium tell me that they have left her there
annotations.note: Sunium is the southern cape of Attica, the last landfall before home. The ship is the sacred vessel Athens sent each year to Delos; while it was away the city had to stay ritually clean and nobody could be executed. The opening of [[pha1|the Phaedo]] explains the custom, and why it gave Socrates his unexpected weeks.

annotations.quote: The third day hence to fertile Phthia shalt thou go
annotations.note: A line from the Iliad, where Achilles threatens to quit the war and sail home to Phthia. Socrates hears it as a promise that dying is a homecoming. I like that he trusts the dream over Crito's harbour gossip about when the ship will dock, and that the man accused of impiety is the one taking a vision seriously.

annotations.quote: that I should be thought to value money more than the life of a friend
annotations.note: Crito's first argument is about Crito. It is easy to smile at, but in Athens reputation was not vanity; it was most of what a man had. Still, the appeal to what 'the many' will believe is exactly the opening Socrates needs.

annotations.quote: for they cannot make a man either wise or foolish; and whatever they do is the result of chance
annotations.note: The dialogue's deepest claim, dropped in passing. If the only real harm is becoming a worse person, then a crowd that can kill you still cannot touch what matters. Crito says 'I will not dispute with you' and moves on, which is a sign he has heard this before and never quite believed it.

annotations.quote: one of them, Simmias the Theban, has brought a large sum of money for this very purpose
annotations.note: Simmias and Cebes are worth remembering. They are the two young men who will do most of the arguing with Socrates on his last day, in the Phaedo. Here they are simply out-of-towners with cash, ready to bribe a way out.

annotations.quote: But you appear to be choosing the easier part, not the better and manlier
annotations.note: A startling charge: that dying is the lazy option and escape the brave one. Crito turns Socrates' own vocabulary of virtue against him. It stings because it is not absurd; a father who lets himself be executed does leave others to finish his work.

annotations.quote: for the time of deliberation is over, and there is only one thing to be done
annotations.note: Crito wants a decision without a discussion. Socrates' whole reply, beginning with the next speech, is a refusal of this sentence: for him the time of deliberation is never over, least of all the night before.

links.why: The trial that put him in this cell; Crito keeps referring back to what Socrates said in court, including his refusal of exile.
The Phaedo opens by explaining the ship from Delos and the delay it caused, and Simmias and Cebes reappear there as the chief questioners.
Socrates' offhand reply about the many becomes a full argument in the next section.

cr2.essay:
Here Socrates takes Crito's panic and turns it, gently, into a procedure. The first move is the one I admire most: 'your zeal is invaluable, if a right one.' He does not say Crito is wrong. He says they do not yet know, and that the only way to find out is to test today's emergency against what the two of them agreed on when nothing was at stake. Either those old conclusions were sound, in which case they still bind, or they were 'talk for the sake of talking.' The cell becomes a trial of whether a lifetime of conversation meant anything.

Two premises get rebuilt. The first is that in matters of right and wrong one should heed the person who knows, not the crowd, as an athlete listens to his trainer and not to the spectators. I have never been fully comfortable with this analogy. We can tell who the good trainers are because their athletes win; who is the corresponding expert on justice? Socrates spent much of the [[ap1|Apology]] reporting that he had searched for such a person and found none, himself included. His phrasing here quietly concedes the difficulty: we must attend to the one who understands 'and what the truth will say.' The expert turns out to be the argument itself. That is a narrower claim than 'ignore the majority', and a more defensible one.

The second premise is the radical one, and Jowett's churchly English ('render evil for evil') makes it sound more familiar than it was. One must never do wrong, not even in return for a wrong. The ordinary Greek view was that a good man helps his friends and harms his enemies; Socrates throws out the second half. He knows how strange this is. He stops to warn Crito that almost nobody has ever believed it, that those who do and those who do not 'have no common ground', and he asks him more than once whether he really means his yes. I take that warning as a piece of honesty on Plato's part. The conclusion of the Crito follows only for someone who accepts this premise, and the text says so.

Then the section ends on a small, exact failure. Socrates asks whether escaping would wrong anyone, and Crito answers, 'I cannot tell, Socrates, for I do not know.' He has agreed to every step and cannot take the last one himself. Everything in [[cr3|the speech of the Laws]] is addressed to that sentence, and when weighing the speech I think it matters to remember whom it was composed for.

annotations.quote: your zeal is invaluable, if a right one; but if wrong, the greater the zeal the greater the danger
annotations.note: The kindest possible way of telling a friend he may be dangerously mistaken. It also states a view of the emotions that runs through all these dialogues: good intentions have no value of their own until someone has checked where they point.

annotations.quote: frightening us like children with hobgoblin terrors
annotations.note: The Greek alludes to Mormo, a bogey that nurses used to scare children into behaving; 'hobgoblin' is Jowett's English nursery equivalent. Prison, confiscation and death are filed under things that frighten children. He said much the same to the jury, and here he says it with the sentence already passed.

annotations.quote: Now you, Crito, are not going to die to-morrow
annotations.note: A joke, and a pointed one. Socrates pretends that Crito is the disinterested party and therefore the better judge, when the whole scene has shown that Crito is the one whose judgment is shaken. The condemned man is the calm one in the room.

annotations.quote: that principle in us which may be assumed to be improved by justice and deteriorated by injustice
annotations.note: A roundabout phrase, and the roundaboutness is in the original: Socrates conspicuously does not say 'soul' here, only 'that in us, whatever it is'. 'Principle' is Jowett's filler. The argument needs just one thing granted, that wrongdoing damages the doer, and it avoids committing to any theory of what gets damaged.

annotations.quote: but the many can kill us
annotations.note: Socrates raises the obvious objection himself, in the objector's voice, and then simply agrees: 'it is true.' He does not pretend the threat away. He only denies that it bears on the question, which is a different and much harder thing to say from inside a death cell.

annotations.quote: that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued
annotations.note: The hinge of the dialogue in eleven words. Once Crito grants this, staying alive stops being an argument for anything, and the only question left is whether escape would be right. Notice how quickly he grants it.

annotations.quote: For this opinion has never been held, and never will be held, by any considerable number of persons
