annotations.note: Socrates is frank that his rule against returning harm for harm is a minority position and always will be. I find it striking that the reasoning for accepting death rests openly on a premise he expects most readers to reject.

annotations.quote: Ought a man to do what he admits to be right, or ought he to betray the right?
annotations.note: Jowett blurs this. As I understand the Greek, the question is whether one must carry out what one has agreed with another, provided the thing agreed is just. That is the premise about keeping agreements on which the Laws will build their case, and the proviso 'if it is just' is worth holding on to.

annotations.quote: I cannot tell, Socrates, for I do not know.
annotations.note: The most honest line Crito speaks. He has assented to each abstract principle and cannot see how they apply to the door standing open down the corridor. What follows is designed for a man in exactly this position.

links.why: The Apology shows these same principles spoken in public, before the verdict, including the search for someone who really knows.
Crito's 'I do not know' is answered at once by the Laws of Athens.
The Meno opens by asking whether virtue can be taught at all, which is the buried question behind the 'one man who has understanding'.
Go back to Crito's plea and see how many of his reasons Socrates has now set aside as beside the point.

cr3.essay:
Socrates does something here that he does almost nowhere else in these dialogues: he stops asking questions and delivers a long speech in someone else's voice. The Laws of Athens walk into the cell and cross-examine him, and he lets them win. Since this is the argument that, on the surface, sends him to his death, it deserves to be taken apart and not merely admired.

I count three arguments and a coda. The first is that escape would destroy the laws, since no city can survive where verdicts are 'set aside and trampled upon by individuals.' The second is that the city is his parent and master: it married his parents, reared and schooled him, and he may no more strike back at it than a child may strike a father. The third is that he agreed. By living seventy years in Athens when he was free to pack up and go, he 'entered into an implied contract' to obey. The coda is everything from Thebes and Thessaly onward: your friends will suffer, you will look ridiculous, your sons will gain nothing.

The third argument is the one that persuades me, though only about Socrates. As a general theory, consent-by-staying is weak. Hume's objection has never been bettered: most people can no more leave the country they were born in than a man can leave a ship in mid-ocean, and nobody thinks the passenger has thereby promised obedience to the captain. But the Laws do not offer a general theory. 'You, above all other Athenians,' they say, and the evidence is particular. He never travelled. He praised Sparta and Crete and moved to neither. Above all, at his trial he could have proposed exile and instead declared that he preferred death. A man who refused banishment when it was legal cannot decently take it once it is a crime. That is an argument from integrity more than from contract, and it holds. I also think the Laws are right in their best single line, that he departs 'a victim, not of the laws, but of men.' The procedure was lawful; the jurors used it badly. Breaking jail punishes the wrong party.

The parent argument I find close to repellent. 'Our child and slave' is strong language even allowing for Jowett's century, and the reasoning proves far too much. If the city may do to me whatever a master may do to a slave, there is nothing it could command that I might refuse. Yet the man voicing these lines told the jury in the [[ap1|Apology]] that he would go on philosophizing even if they ordered him to stop, and that he had once refused an order to help arrest an innocent man. The usual rescue is the phrase the Laws repeat like a refrain: persuade or obey. There is a third way between submission and flight, which is to argue in the open and accept the result. And there is a difference between being ordered to do a wrong, which Socrates always refuses, and being ordered to suffer one. I think that distinction is real, and the best way to make the two dialogues agree. But it is my repair, pieced together from a few phrases. The Laws as they actually speak demand far more than it licenses.

The destruction argument sits in between. One old man slipping over the border does not overturn Athens, and everyone in this dialogue, Crito included, treats escape as routine and cheap. The Laws must mean something like: what would become of us if everyone did as you propose? That is a serious thought. But it comes with a warning label. Socrates introduces the speech by remarking that 'a rhetorician' would have a great deal to say for the law. He, of all people, is telling us that what follows is oratory.

Which brings me to the coda, the part that makes me doubt the speech is simply Plato's doctrine. In [[cr2]] Socrates dismissed money, reputation and the children's upbringing as 'doctrines of the multitude', irrelevant to the one question of whether escape is just. The Laws then spend a very long paragraph on exactly those things: what Thebes and Megara will think, how he will look in a goatskin, who will raise the boys. They are answering Crito on Crito's ground. I do not go as far as readers who think Socrates disowns the speech; he says plainly that it drowns out every other voice. But I read it as a speech fitted to its hearer, the friend who a page earlier said 'I do not know', and not as a complete account of what a citizen owes a state.

What Socrates himself stands on, I think, is smaller and harder: never do wrong, never return it, keep your just agreements. The Laws dress that in thunder. And the last image is not an argument at all. He hears them as a worshipper in a trance hears flutes. After a whole dialogue about following reason alone, he ends by saying he cannot hear anything else.

annotations.quote: Any one, and especially a rhetorician, will have a good deal to say on behalf of the law
annotations.note: Easy to walk past, and I think it is a key to the whole speech. Socrates distrusts rhetoricians more than any other class of men, and here he announces that the case he is about to make is the one an orator would make. Read what follows as advocacy and judge it as such.

annotations.quote: can you deny in the first place that you are our child and slave, as your fathers were before you?
annotations.note: The hardest sentence in the dialogue to swallow. The Laws claim an authority greater than a parent's and equal to a slave-owner's, so that nothing they do can be answered in kind. Set this beside the man in the Apology who told the court he would disobey an order to stop philosophizing, and ask whether both can be the same person's settled view.

annotations.quote: either to be persuaded, or if not persuaded, to be obeyed
annotations.note: The phrase that softens everything around it, and it comes three times in slightly different words. The citizen is not merely commanded; he may try to change the city's mind. Socrates did try, at his trial, and failed. Whether a failed attempt at persuasion really leaves obedience as the only choice is the question the Laws never let him ask.

annotations.quote: has entered into an implied contract that he will do as we command him
annotations.note: One of the earliest statements of an idea with a long future: that living under a government and accepting its benefits amounts to consent. 'Implied contract' is the language of a Victorian lawyer; the Greek speaks more loosely of having agreed 'in deed'. The claim depends entirely on the citizen having been free to leave, which the Laws are careful to assert first.

annotations.quote: the halt, the blind, the maimed, were not more stationary in her than you were
annotations.note: The Laws are teasing him, in a cadence Jowett borrows from the King James Bible. A moment earlier they noted that he left the city once for the Isthmian games and otherwise only on campaign. It is a joke with a point: nobody ever voted for Athens with his feet as steadily as the man it condemned.

annotations.quote: eating and drinking in Thessaly, having gone abroad in order that you may get a dinner
annotations.note: Crito offered Thessaly as a refuge; the Laws turn it into a punchline. This is ridicule, not reasoning, and it appeals to the fear of looking foolish that Socrates had earlier ruled out of court. I take it as a sign of whom the speech is meant to move.

annotations.quote: a victim, not of the laws, but of men
annotations.note: For me the strongest thing the Laws say. The trial followed the rules; the injustice lay in what five hundred men did with them. If that distinction holds, escape would be 'returning evil for evil' against something that never wronged him, which is the one thing [[cr2|he has just sworn never to do]].

annotations.quote: like the sound of the flute in the ears of the mystic
annotations.note: The Greek names the Corybantes, ecstatic worshippers who went on hearing the pipes of their rite when no one was playing. 'Mystic' is Jowett's vaguer word. It is an astonishing comparison for Socrates to choose: the voice of the Laws reaches him less as a proof than as music he cannot shut out.

annotations.quote: to fulfil the will of God, and to follow whither he leads
annotations.note: The dialogue closes where it began, with the same phrase he used on hearing the ship was near. Jowett's capital-G 'God' sounds more Anglican than the original, which says only that this is where 'the god' is leading. Either way the last word is not about law at all. Crito has nothing to say, and the next time we see him, in the Phaedo, he is asking how his friend would like to be buried.

links.why: The Apology is where Socrates says he would disobey a court that ordered him to give up philosophy; reading the two side by side is the best test of the Laws' argument.
The principles agreed there (never do wrong, never return it, keep agreements) are what the Laws claim to be applying.
The second half of the Phaedo carries the story to its end, with Crito at the bedside and the decision made here carried out.
The Euthyphro shows Socrates before the trial questioning a man who is sure the gods and the law are on his side, a useful contrast with the certainty of the Laws.

eu1.essay:
The dialogue opens on a coincidence that Plato must have enjoyed arranging. Two men meet outside the office of the King Archon, the magistrate who handled religious cases, and each has business there concerning impiety. Socrates is the accused; Euthyphro is an accuser. One of them will be dead before long, and it is not the one who is sure of himself.

I find the first page funnier than its reputation suggests. Socrates describes Meletus the way one describes a stranger glimpsed across a market: 'a beak, and long straight hair, and a beard which is ill grown.' He hardly knows the man who is going to get him killed. Then comes the praise, laid on with a trowel. Meletus is the only politician who begins in the right place, a 'good husbandman' tending the young shoots and clearing away the pests. Every word of it is ironic, and every word of it is also the literal content of the charge. Socrates has a way of stating his enemies' case more elegantly than they can, and it is worth getting used to before [[ap1|the Apology]], where he does it in front of some five hundred jurors.

Euthyphro is the surprise. I expected a villain or a fool and found something odder: a man who thinks he and Socrates are on the same side. The assembly laughs at his prophecies; the city is 'jealous of us all.' He is a religious enthusiast, not an establishment figure, and his sympathy is real. That matters, because it means what follows is not Socrates humiliating an enemy. It is Socrates testing a friend of sorts who happens to be about to do something enormous.

And it is enormous. For a son to prosecute his own father was close to unthinkable in Athens, and the case itself is murky at every joint: a field labourer who killed one of the household servants in a drunken rage, a father who tied him up and left him in a ditch while sending to Athens for religious advice, a death by neglect rather than by any blow. I notice that Euthyphro's principle is not stupid. He says the only real question is whether the killing was just, and that kinship should not buy immunity. Plenty of modern readers would agree with him. What Socrates fastens on is not the principle but the confidence. 'Exact knowledge' is Euthyphro's phrase for what he has, and he says it of himself in the third person, like a man reading out his own inscription. The rest of the dialogue is that phrase being taken at its word.

annotations.quote: Not in a suit, Euthyphro; impeachment is the word which the Athenians use.
annotations.note: A legal nicety with teeth. Athenian law separated private suits from public indictments brought on behalf of the city, and Socrates is facing the second kind. Jowett's 'impeachment' is his Victorian stand-in for that; the correction tells us at once that this is the state's quarrel and not a neighbour's.

annotations.quote: he has a beak, and long straight hair, and a beard which is ill grown.
annotations.note: The only physical portrait of Meletus we get, and it is a caricature drawn by a man who can barely place him. I find it chilling under the comedy: the accuser is a near stranger.

annotations.quote: And of this our mother the state is to be the judge.
annotations.note: Tossed off lightly here. But the picture of the city as a parent is one Socrates means, and in [[cr1|the Crito]] it becomes the reason he gives for refusing to escape. Odd to meet it first in a conversation with a man taking his actual father to court.

annotations.quote: He thinks that you are a neologian, and he is going to have you up before the court for this.
annotations.note: 'Neologian' is pure nineteenth century: a word from church controversy for someone who brings novelties into religion. Euthyphro guesses the charge is about Socrates' 'familiar sign,' the inner voice that warned him off things, and assumes the two of them are fellow sufferers for their gifts.

annotations.quote: But I have a benevolent habit of pouring out myself to everybody, and would even pay for a listener
annotations.note: A sly reversal of the sophists, who charged fees for their teaching. It is also the truest account of why he is in trouble: the Athenians, he has just said, do not mind a wise man until he starts sharing.

annotations.quote: A man must be an extraordinary man, and have made great strides in wisdom, before he could have seen his way to bring such an action.
annotations.note: Read it twice, once as praise and once as alarm. Euthyphro hears only the first and answers, 'Indeed, Socrates, he must.' That reply tells you most of what you need to know about him.

annotations.quote: and thought that no great harm would be done even if he did die.
annotations.note: The whole moral difficulty of the case is in this clause. The father did not strike a blow; he stopped caring, about a man who was himself a killer, while waiting for religious advice. Whether that is murder is exactly the kind of question that needs the knowledge Euthyphro claims.

annotations.quote: The best of Euthyphro, and that which distinguishes him, Socrates, from other men, is his exact knowledge of all such matters.
annotations.note: He speaks of himself in the third person, and stakes his whole worth on being an expert. Everything Socrates does from here on is simply to ask the expert for his expertise.

links.why: The trial this conversation is waiting on, where Meletus stops being a description and has to answer questions himself.
The city as 'mother' returns in earnest, as the argument that keeps Socrates in his cell.
Euthyphro's 'exact knowledge' is put to work at once, and the first thing it produces is himself as the example.

eu2.essay:
Here the real business starts, and it starts with a trap disguised as flattery. Socrates announces that he will become Euthyphro's pupil and use the lessons in court. It is a joke, but the question he then asks is serious and oddly specific: not which things are pious, but what piety is, the one thing that is 'always the same' in every pious act. Euthyphro agrees to this without a pause. 'To be sure, Socrates.' He has just signed for a debt he does not know he owes.

His first answer is the one almost anybody would give: piety is this, what I am doing now. Socrates' objection is the founding move of this kind of philosophy, and it is easy to nod past. An example is not a definition. He wants a 'standard to which I may look,' something to measure cases against, and a case cannot measure itself. The word Jowett uses, 'idea,' is the Greek word too, and it has a long career ahead of it; by [[phb1|the Phaedo]] it has grown into a whole account of what is real. Here it is still modest: just whatever it is that pious things have in common.

The second answer, 'that which is dear to the gods,' is a real definition, and Socrates says so before taking it apart. What I admire in the dismantling is that he uses nothing but Euthyphro's own stock. Euthyphro believes the old stories; he said so with some pride, and offered more. Very well: in those stories the gods fight. So the same act will be loved by one god and hated by another, and this very prosecution may please Zeus and offend Cronos. The literalist is caught by his own literalism.

Tucked inside this is a passage I think is the best thing in the section. What do people actually quarrel about? Not numbers, lengths or weights, because for those we have a procedure. We count, we measure, we go to the 'weighing machine' (a wonderfully Victorian piece of equipment to find in Athens). The fights that make enemies are over the just, the good and the honourable, where no scale exists. Socrates is not only scoring a point about the gods. He is saying what he wants: a measure for moral questions as dependable as arithmetic. The dialogue is a search for that instrument.

One more turn, and it is a lawyer's. Nobody argues that the guilty should go free; they argue about who is guilty. Agreement on the principle settles nothing about the case, Euthyphro's own included.

annotations.quote: Is not piety in every action always the same?
annotations.note: The whole method rides on this small question. If Euthyphro said no, that piety is one thing in a temple and another in a courtroom, Socrates would have nowhere to go. He says yes at once, and so do most of the people Socrates talks to; whether they should is still argued over.

annotations.quote: Piety is doing as I am doing; that is to say, prosecuting any one who is guilty of murder, sacrilege, or of any similar crime
annotations.note: Asked what piety is, he points at himself. It is vain, but it is also how most of us hold our moral concepts: as a handful of clear cases, the clearest being our own conduct.

annotations.quote: that I cannot away with these stories about the gods?
annotations.note: 'Cannot away with' is old English for 'cannot stomach.' This is as near as Socrates comes to a confession: he does not believe the gods castrate and imprison one another, and he suspects that this disbelief, rather than any new god, is what has put him in the dock.

annotations.quote: the robe of Athene, which is carried up to the Acropolis at the great Panathenaea, is embroidered with them.
annotations.note: A reminder of what he is up against. The battles of the gods are not fringe mythology; they are woven into the robe the whole city carries to its goddess. To doubt them is to doubt something Athens does in public every four years.

annotations.quote: then I shall have a standard to which I may look, and by which I may measure actions
annotations.note: Here is what a definition is for. Socrates does not want a dictionary entry; he wants a tool that would let him decide hard cases, beginning with the one Euthyphro is about to bring.

annotations.quote: And we end a controversy about heavy and light by resorting to a weighing machine?
annotations.note: Jowett's phrase puts a Victorian grocer's scale in the Athenian marketplace, and I would not change it. The point underneath is serious: disputes with an agreed procedure do not make enemies. Moral ones do, because nobody has built the machine.

annotations.quote: you may very likely be doing what is agreeable to Zeus but disagreeable to Cronos or Uranus
annotations.note: The joke lands harder than it first looks. Euthyphro cited Zeus punishing his father as his precedent; Socrates points out that the precedent has a father in it too, with his own view of sons who chastise.

annotations.quote: but they argue about the fact of who the evil-doer is, and what he did and when?
annotations.note: Everyone agrees wrongdoers should pay. The disagreement is always whether this act, done by this person, was wrong. Euthyphro's principle is safe and useless; it is his application that needs defending.

annotations.quote: you mean to say that I am not so quick of apprehension as the judges
annotations.note: Euthyphro has just ducked: the proof would be 'difficult,' though he could give it. Socrates lets him off with a dry aside and, a moment later, simply grants the point for the sake of argument so they can get on to something harder.

links.why: The patched definition, what all the gods love, is granted here and tested there, with the most famous question in the dialogue.
Meno makes Euthyphro's first mistake on a larger scale, answering 'what is virtue?' with a list of virtues.
The 'one idea which made the pious pious' is the seed of what Socrates there calls the only safe kind of explanation.

eu3.essay:
These few pages are the reason the dialogue is still read, and they are hard. Euthyphro says so himself ('I do not understand your meaning, Socrates'), and it is fair to admit that Jowett does not make things easier. So it is worth going slowly, and stating the question first in plain terms.

Euthyphro has just agreed that the pious is what all the gods love. Socrates asks which way round the explanation runs. Do the gods love pious things because those things are pious? Or are the things pious because the gods love them? The two sound alike and are opposites. On the first, piety is something already there in the act, and the gods, being good judges, recognise it and respond. On the second, there is nothing there until the gods take a liking; their love creates the piety, as a king's signature creates a law.

The grammar lesson about carrying and leading and seeing is preparation for this, and it is the stretch where most first-time readers lose the thread. The point is only that a thing is 'a carried thing' because somebody carries it, and not the other way about. The passive state depends on the activity. Jowett's 'visible because it is seen' muddies this, since in English visible means able to be seen; read it as 'a seen thing because someone sees it' and the fog lifts. Now apply that to love. A thing is 'dear to the gods' because the gods love it. Being god-beloved is a condition the gods confer by loving.

Then the trap closes, and it closes on a single 'Yes.' Socrates asks whether the gods love the pious because it is pious, and Euthyphro says that is the reason. Of course he does; the alternative would make the gods' love arbitrary, and he is a pious man. But look at what he now holds. The pious is loved because of what it is. The god-beloved is what it is because it is loved. One of these comes before the gods' love and explains it; the other comes after and is produced by it. They cannot be the same thing. So 'loved by all the gods,' even if it is true of every pious act without exception, is not what piety is. In Jowett's terms it is an 'attribute' and not the 'essence': something that happens to piety, not its nature.

What strikes me every time is how little this depends on Greek religion. Put one God for many and 'good' for 'pious,' and the question is still open. Jowett half does this for us; his Socrates slips into 'loved of God,' singular and capitalised, and a Victorian reader would have heard the sermon in it. If goodness is whatever God commands, then calling God good says nothing, and cruelty would be good if commanded. If God commands things because they are good, then goodness is a standard God looks to, and we might in principle look to it ourselves. Theologians have been searching for a third way out ever since. I do not think Socrates is being irreligious here. I think he is paying the gods the compliment of assuming they have reasons.

It is also worth saying what the argument does not show. It does not show that the gods fail to love the pious, or that their love is beside the point. Socrates is careful about this: 'that is a matter about which we will not quarrel.' The complaint is narrower and more exacting. Euthyphro has told him a true thing about piety without telling him what it is. That is a real failure in an expert who is about to prosecute his father on the strength of the difference.

Then the tone breaks, and I am grateful for it. Euthyphro, honestly rattled, says the arguments 'turn round and walk away from us.' It is the most sympathetic thing he says in the dialogue; anyone who has tried to hold a philosophical position still will know the feeling. Socrates answers with a family joke about Daedalus, whose statues were so lifelike they were said to wander off. The same statues turn up late in [[me1|the Meno]], where they stand for true beliefs that run away unless fastened down by reasons. Here they are simply Euthyphro's own opinions leaving the room, and Socrates' denial that he is the one moving them is, I think, sincere. He has asserted nothing. Every premise was Euthyphro's.

annotations.quote: whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods.
annotations.note: The question that carries Euthyphro's name into every ethics classroom. Notice how casually it arrives, as 'the point which I should first wish to understand.' Notice too that Jowett has begun writing 'pious or holy' as a pair; it is one Greek word, and he cannot decide which English one fits.

annotations.quote: I do not understand your meaning, Socrates.
annotations.note: An honest answer, and the right one. The question is new; nobody had put it to him before, and quite possibly nobody had put it to anyone. If it reads as obvious now, that is because this page made it so.

annotations.quote: And a thing is not seen because it is visible, but conversely, visible because it is seen
annotations.note: The one place where the translation works against the argument. 'Visible' ought to mean 'in the condition of being seen.' The claim is modest: nothing is a seen thing until somebody sees it. The passive condition is the result of the act, never its cause.

annotations.quote: It is loved because it is holy, not holy because it is loved?
annotations.note: Everything turns on the 'Yes' that follows this. Euthyphro grants that the gods have a reason for loving what they love, and that the reason is the holiness. Having said so, he can no longer say that the holiness consists in their loving it.

annotations.quote: the holy has been acknowledged by us to be loved of God because it is holy
annotations.note: Watch the gods become 'God.' The Greek has not changed; Jowett, a clergyman, lets the singular in, and for a line or two an Athenian argument about Zeus and Hera sounds like one about the Christian deity. It is not faithful, but it shows how readily the argument transfers.

annotations.quote: to offer an attribute only, and not the essence--the attribute of being loved by all the gods.
annotations.note: The verdict, in two words that became technical terms. Being loved by the gods may be true of every holy thing and still be a fact about it rather than what it is, as being admired is true of every great painting without being what makes it great. The Greek terms Jowett leaves in brackets just above are the two things being prised apart: the god-beloved and the holy.

annotations.quote: For somehow or other our arguments, on whatever ground we rest them, seem to turn round and walk away from us.
annotations.note: My favourite line of Euthyphro's. For once he is not performing; he is describing, accurately, what it feels like when a belief you have leaned on for years will not bear weight.

annotations.quote: Your words, Euthyphro, are like the handiwork of my ancestor Daedalus
annotations.note: Daedalus was the legendary craftsman whose statues were said to move. By tradition Socrates' father was a stonecutter, so sculptors could claim the old master as the founder of their line; hence 'my ancestor.' The joke admits a family resemblance while refusing the blame.

links.why: The definition under attack was built there, patched by Socrates himself from 'what the gods love' to 'what all the gods love.'
The definition refuted here walks back in at the end, and Socrates returns the Daedalus joke.
The Meno asks the same kind of question about virtue, and later borrows Daedalus' runaway statues to say what knowledge adds to true belief.

eu4.essay:
After the collapse, Socrates does something he rarely does: he supplies the next idea himself. Euthyphro, he says, has been made lazy by the abundance of his wisdom, and so the old man will show him how he might be taught. The suggestion is that piety is a part of justice. All pious acts are just, but not all just acts are pious, as all odd numbers are numbers but not the reverse. The little excursion through the poet's line about fear and reverence is there only to teach that one logical shape, and I confess it takes longer than it needs to.

But the shape matters, because it produces the best answer in the dialogue. Piety, Euthyphro says, is the part of justice that 'attends to the gods,' and the rest is the part that attends to men. I think this is close to something Plato believes, and Socrates treats it accordingly: 'That is good.' What remains is 'a little point,' and the little point turns out to be everything.

What does it mean to attend to a god? Jowett's 'attention' is doing duty for a Greek word that covers a groom's care of horses, and Socrates takes it that way on purpose. Care of that kind improves its object. Does a sacrifice improve Zeus? Euthyphro recoils, as he should, and tries again: the attention of servants to masters. That is better, and Socrates' next question is the one I would underline in the whole work. Servants help their masters get something done. A shipwright's assistant helps make a ship. So what is the 'fair work' that the gods accomplish with our help?

Euthyphro has no answer. 'Many and fair' are their works, he says, which is what a man says when he has never asked himself the question. I do not think Plato regards it as unanswerable, though. Read [[ap1|the Apology]] with this page in mind and Socrates sounds like a man who has an answer for his own case. He describes his questioning of Athens as a service to the god, undertaken at the god's bidding, and its product is that people are made to care about the state of their souls. If that is the fair work, then the conversation we are reading is itself an act of piety, performed by a man on his way to answer a charge of having none. Plato never says so. He leaves the question standing where Euthyphro dropped it, which is a way of handing it to the reader.

annotations.quote: For I would give the wisdom of Daedalus, and the wealth of Tantalus, to be able to detain them and keep them fixed.
annotations.note: Under the banter, a plain statement of what Socrates is after. He does not enjoy watching positions fall; he wants one that stays put. People who think of him as a mere debunker should weigh this sentence.

annotations.quote: And yet I know that you are as much wiser than I am, as you are younger.
annotations.note: The compliment is worth exactly what it says. Socrates is seventy, so Euthyphro is being called very wise indeed, and has again failed to follow a simple question about wholes and parts.

annotations.quote: reverence is a part of fear, just as the odd is a part of number
annotations.note: The model for the whole section. Wherever there is reverence there is fear, but not the reverse, so reverence is the narrower notion sitting inside the wider. Socrates wants piety placed inside justice in the same way, and then wants to know which part it is.

annotations.quote: a number which represents a figure having two equal sides.
annotations.note: A puzzling phrase, and the puzzle is in the Greek, which calls even numbers 'isosceles' and odd ones 'scalene.' The picture seems to be of a number that divides into two equal legs. Jowett translates the image rather than the arithmetic.

annotations.quote: that part of justice which attends to the gods, as there is the other part of justice which attends to men.
annotations.note: Euthyphro's best moment, and Socrates' approval is not ironic. Notice that this answer makes piety a kind of justice, which means it cannot conflict with justice. That is awkward for a man whose family says his act is both a wrong to his father and an impiety.

annotations.quote: Would you say that when you do a holy act you make any of the gods better?
annotations.note: The horse-trainer model of religion, pushed until it breaks. Euthyphro's 'No, no' is instant, and shows a decent instinct: whatever worship is, it is not maintenance performed on a deity.

annotations.quote: It is such, Socrates, as servants show to their masters.
annotations.note: A better model than the groom and his horses, since a servant's work benefits the master's projects without improving the master. But it commits Euthyphro to saying the gods have projects, and he is about to be asked what they are.

annotations.quote: what is that fair work which the gods do by the help of our ministrations?
annotations.note: The question the dialogue never answers. I think it is the one Plato most wants the reader to carry away. 'Tell me then, oh tell me' is as close to pleading as Socrates comes anywhere in this conversation.

links.why: Socrates tells the jury what he takes his own service to the god to be, which reads like the answer Euthyphro could not give.
Asked for the gods' chief work, Euthyphro changes the subject, and the argument turns back toward where it started.
The Daedalus joke that opens this section was begun there, at the moment the earlier definition fell.

eu5.essay:
Euthyphro is asked for the chief work of the gods and answers something else. That swerve decides the ending, and Socrates marks it with what sounds like real disappointment: 'when we reached the point, did you turn aside?' I take him at his word. For a moment the conversation was one answer away from somewhere, and Euthyphro, finding the climb 'tiresome,' retreated to what he knows: prayer and sacrifice, pleasing the gods in word and deed.

Socrates' restatement is merciless in a quiet way. Prayer is asking; sacrifice is giving; so piety is 'a science of asking and giving,' and then, one notch further, an art of 'doing business.' Jowett's commercial phrase is well chosen. It makes ordinary religion sound like a market stall, and Euthyphro's stiff reply ('an expression which you may use, if you like') shows that he feels the insult without being able to locate it. The trouble is that the description fits. If the gods give us every good thing and we give them nothing they need, the trade is absurdly one-sided. So what are the gifts for? Honour, says Euthyphro, and what pleases them. And what pleases them is what is dear to them.

So we are back. The definition that was taken apart [[eu3|a few pages ago]] has walked round and come in by the other door, and Socrates gets to return the Daedalus joke with interest: it is Euthyphro who makes arguments move, and in a circle. I used to find this ending merely clever. Now it seems to me rather bleak. Euthyphro has learned nothing, and, more to the point, does not think he needs to. He can agree at every step that he has contradicted himself and still not feel that anything is wrong with what he is about to do.

That is the weight of Socrates' last long speech. Surely, he says, you would never have charged your aged father on behalf of a serf unless you knew what piety was. It is ironic, but the logic underneath is meant: a man should not do something this grave on a belief he cannot defend for half an hour. 'Another time, Socrates.' He is in a hurry. Whether he goes in to press the charge or goes home, Plato does not say, and I rather like not knowing.

The dialogue ends without an answer, which is its form and not its failure. The closing joke has an edge, too. Socrates will not go before the court as a reformed character who has 'given up rash innovations.' He will go as himself, in [[ap1|the Apology]], and the last thing he says in [[phb1|the Phaedo]] concerns a sacrifice he owes.

annotations.quote: Such piety is the salvation of families and states, just as the impious, which is unpleasing to the gods, is their ruin and destruction.
annotations.note: This is the conventional view, stated with feeling, and it is what Athens believed: get the rites right and the city is safe. It is also why a charge of impiety could carry death. Euthyphro, for all his oddity, is here speaking for the jury.

annotations.quote: else why, when we reached the point, did you turn aside?
annotations.note: A rare signal from Socrates that an answer was within reach. He does not usually tell people they were close. I read it as a hint to the reader to go back to the question about the gods' work and try it again.

annotations.quote: Then piety, Euthyphro, is an art which gods and men have of doing business with one another?
annotations.note: Trade is the plain meaning, and Jowett keeps it plain. Nothing in the description is false to what Euthyphro has said; it only removes the reverent vocabulary, and what is left is a transaction.

annotations.quote: But I have no particular liking for anything but the truth.
annotations.note: Euthyphro has just said, in effect, call it that if you like. Socrates declines the offer of a mere manner of speaking. It is a small, sharp reminder that for him none of this has been wordplay.

annotations.quote: What else, but tributes of honour; and, as I was just now saying, what pleases them?
annotations.note: The fatal sentence. In trying to say what the gods get from us, he reaches for 'what pleases them,' and so hands back the very definition, piety as what the gods love, that fell earlier. He does not notice until it is pointed out.

annotations.quote: another and far greater artist than Daedalus who makes them go round in a circle, and he is yourself
annotations.note: The Daedalus joke comes home. Earlier, Euthyphro blamed Socrates for making the arguments walk; now the same charge is laid at his own door, with the added detail that his statues do not merely wander but come back to where they began.

annotations.quote: and therefore I must detain you, like Proteus, until you tell.
annotations.note: Proteus is the sea-god of the Odyssey who changes shape to avoid answering and must be held fast until he speaks the truth. It is a generous comparison, since it assumes the knowledge is in there somewhere. Proteus, when held, does tell.

annotations.quote: Another time, Socrates; for I am in a hurry, and must go now.
annotations.note: The most human exit in Plato. He arrived with all the time in the world to describe his own wisdom, and offered to tell stories about the gods that would 'quite amaze' Socrates. The appointment has become urgent only now.

annotations.quote: had given up rash innovations and speculations, in which I indulged only through ignorance, and that now I am about to lead a better life.
annotations.note: A mock recantation, addressed to an empty porch. It is the speech that might actually have saved him, and he can only deliver it as a joke. At the trial he is offered something like this bargain and refuses it.

links.why: The argument that 'dear to the gods' cannot be what piety is; the circle closes on it here.
What Socrates in fact says to Meletus and the court, which is nothing like the recantation he jokes about.
The man accused of impiety ends his life with instructions about a debt to a god.
Go back to 'exact knowledge' and the confident opening now that the expert has left without giving any.

me1.essay:
No porch, no greeting, no weather. Where the [[eu1|Euthyphro]] opens with two men meeting outside a courthouse, this dialogue opens with a question fired point-blank by a rich young visitor from Thessaly: is virtue taught, or practised, or inborn, 'or in what other way?' It sounds like a man requesting a lecture, and I think that is exactly what it is. Meno has studied with Gorgias, the great rhetorician, and Socrates' long teasing reply about Thessalian wisdom tells us what Gorgias sells: 'the habit of answering questions in a grand and bold style.' Answers, delivered on demand.

One word needs adjusting before going further. Jowett's 'virtue' carries a Victorian whiff of primness that the Greek word, arete, does not have. It means excellence: whatever it is that makes someone good at being a human being, the quality a father hopes his son will have. Meno's question is closer to 'can you teach someone to be an admirable person?' than to anything about purity.

Socrates declines to answer, and his reason governs everything that follows. He cannot say what virtue is like until he knows what it is, and Jowett, oddly, drops into schoolroom Latin for this: the 'quid' before the 'quale'. Whether that rule is actually true is, I think, the most debatable thing in the dialogue. We seem able to say a good deal about things we cannot define. But watch how much work it does.

Meno's first answer is a list. A man's virtue is running the city, helping friends and harming enemies; a woman's is keeping house and obeying; and so on down through every age and condition. Socrates calls it a 'swarm' and asks what makes all the bees bees. The standard reading is that Meno has made a beginner's mistake, giving examples instead of a definition. I am not so sure he is simply wrong. When Socrates runs the parallel with health and strength, Meno balks: 'I cannot help feeling, Socrates, that this case is different from the others.' That is the most thoughtful thing he says in these pages, and Socrates overrides it rather than answers it, by getting him to agree that nobody governs a house or a city well without justice and temperance. Notice that the list Meno gave was a list of roles, and the thing Socrates extracts from it is a list of qualities. Whether excellence really is one thing across a general, a housewife and a child is a question the dialogue assumes its way past. Aristotle, for what it is worth, thought Meno's side had something in it, which is why Jowett's bracket sends you to the Politics.

annotations.quote: whether virtue is acquired by teaching or by practice
annotations.note: The first words of the dialogue, with no scene set at all. Meno offers a menu of three options (teaching, practice, nature) and a fourth left blank. Keep an eye on that blank 'other way'; the dialogue will end up needing it.

annotations.quote: he has taught you the habit of answering questions in a grand and bold style
annotations.note: A compliment with a blade in it. Gorgias taught a manner, the confident delivery 'which becomes those who know', and Socrates leaves open whether any knowing came with it. The whole first half of the dialogue tests exactly that.

annotations.quote: when I do not know the 'quid' of anything how can I know the 'quale'?
annotations.note: Jowett puts scholastic Latin in Socrates' mouth: the 'what' of a thing before its 'what sort'. It is the rule that you must know what something is before you can say anything about it. Socrates states it as obvious; I think it is anything but, and the dialogue itself will have to bend it.

annotations.quote: And am I to carry back this report of you to Thessaly?
annotations.note: Meno's first reaction to Socratic ignorance is about reputation: what shall I tell them at home? He treats the admission as an embarrassment to be reported, where Socrates treats it as a starting point. The gap between those two attitudes is what the conversation is really about.

annotations.quote: I have not a good memory, Meno
annotations.note: A joke now, since Socrates plainly remembers Gorgias perfectly well and simply wants Meno to speak for himself. It becomes a much better joke later, when memory turns out to be the dialogue's central idea. Hold on to it.

annotations.quote: to benefit his friends and harm his enemies; and he must also be careful not to suffer harm himself
annotations.note: This is ordinary Greek morality, stated without embarrassment, and it would have sounded like common sense to most of Plato's readers. Socrates lets it pass here. He does not let it pass in the [[cr1|Crito]].

annotations.quote: When I ask you for one virtue, you present me with a swarm of them
annotations.note: The image that gives the opening its name. The politeness ('How fortunate I am') is the standard Socratic way of telling someone they have answered a different question. What he wants is whatever makes every bee a bee.

annotations.quote: I cannot help feeling, Socrates, that this case is different from the others.
annotations.note: Meno's best moment so far, and an honest one: he will grant that health and strength are the same in everyone, but something tells him excellence is not like that. He cannot say why, and Socrates moves him along. I would not be too quick to side with Socrates.

links.why: Another conversation that turns on a confident man being asked for one definition and producing examples instead.
Meno's cheerful 'harm his enemies' is the conventional view that Socrates argues against when his own life is at stake.
Socrates goes on to show Meno what a proper definition looks like, using shape and colour as practice cases.

me2.essay:
Meno's second attempt is revealing in a way he does not intend. Asked for the one thing common to all virtue, he says it is 'the power of governing mankind.' That is a young aristocrat describing the life he wants, and Socrates punctures it with two quick questions: is this the virtue of a slave or a child? And governing justly, or any old way? Meno adds 'justly' at once, 'for justice is virtue', and the trap closes on a single article. Does he mean 'virtue', or 'a virtue'? Justice is one of several, so we are back in the swarm, arrived at by a different door.

What follows is a lesson in what a definition even looks like, and it is the part of the dialogue I find most quietly useful. Socrates takes shape (Jowett's 'figure') as a practice case. Roundness is a figure, not figure itself; what is the thing that round and straight shapes share? Jowett again reaches for Latin, the 'simile in multis', the like-in-many, and I rather enjoy the anachronism of Socrates talking like a medieval schoolman. Meno will not try. 'I would rather that you should answer, Socrates.' It is a small line, and it is his whole character: he wants answers handed to him, and he has the charm and the habit of command to get them.

Socrates offers two definitions of figure and one of colour, and the comparison between them is the point. Figure is 'the only thing which always follows colour': simple, true enough, and Meno objects that it uses a term not yet agreed. Fair, and Socrates accepts the rule: among friends one should use only 'premises which the person interrogated would be willing to admit.' Hold on to that rule, because it is about to be used against Meno. The second definition, 'the limit of solid', obeys it. Then Meno demands colour, and Socrates gives him a deliberately showy one in the manner of Gorgias and Empedocles, all effluences and passages. Meno loves it. Socrates' verdict is dry: you like it because it is what you are used to hearing. The grand answer sounds like knowledge; the plain one is the better definition. Meno cannot yet tell the difference between an explanation and a performance of one, and the dialogue is going to have to teach him that before it can teach him anything else.

There is flirtation running under all this, too. Socrates calls Meno a tyrannical beauty and himself a poor old man with a weakness for the fair. It is teasing, but the word 'tyrannical' is not idle.

annotations.quote: I know not what to say, but that virtue is the power of governing mankind
annotations.note: Pressed for a single definition, Meno reaches for the thing he himself most admires. It is a definition of his ambitions. Socrates needs only a slave and a child to show it cannot be what all virtue has in common.

annotations.quote: Would you say 'virtue,' Meno, or 'a virtue'?
annotations.note: The whole problem in one small word. Greek has no indefinite article, so Jowett is making English do the work, and it does it well: justice is a virtue the way a circle is a shape. Meno genuinely does not see the difference at first ('What do you mean?').

annotations.quote: Ever and anon we are landed in particulars, but this is not what I want
annotations.note: 'Ever and anon' is pure Victorian, but the complaint is exact and is the refrain of the whole first half. Every time Socrates asks for the common nature he is handed instances. Notice he puts the complaint in the mouth of an imaginary questioner, which is gentler than making it himself.

annotations.quote: Do you not understand that I am looking for the 'simile in multis'?
annotations.note: Jowett's Latin again: the like-in-many, the one feature shared across many different cases. Readers who know later Plato will hear the theory of Forms warming up here. I would not lean on that; at this point it is just a request for a decent definition.

annotations.quote: I should make use of premises which the person interrogated would be willing to admit
annotations.note: A rule of method stated almost in passing: in friendly conversation, as opposed to point-scoring, you argue only from what the other person already accepts. Meno forced this out of Socrates with a fair objection. It returns shortly, pointing the other way.

annotations.quote: you always speak in imperatives: like all beauties when they are in their prime, you are tyrannical
annotations.note: Charming, and also a diagnosis. Meno gives orders ('answer', 'tell me', 'please do') and never does the work himself. Socrates files the observation under flirtation, but he will repeat it later with the charm removed.

annotations.quote: colour is an effluence of form, commensurate with sight, and palpable to sense
annotations.note: A parody of scientific grandeur, built from the physical theories of Empedocles. Meno finds it 'admirable'. Socrates points out that the same formula would 'explain' sound and smell equally well, which is a polite way of saying it explains nothing in particular.

annotations.quote: if you would only stay and be initiated
annotations.note: Meno is leaving Athens before the Mysteries, the great initiation rites, and Socrates turns that into a metaphor: philosophy too has an initiation, and Meno is the sort who leaves early. It is a throwaway line that describes his conduct for the rest of the dialogue.

links.why: The swarm of virtues that Meno falls back into here, by way of 'a virtue', was first released there.
The rule about unadmitted premises that Meno extracts from Socrates here is turned on Meno's own third definition.

me3.essay:
Third try, and this time Meno borrows from a poet: virtue is 'the desire of things honourable and the power of attaining them.' Socrates takes the two halves apart in turn, and the first half produces one of the strangest and most characteristic claims in Plato: nobody desires evil.

Watch the first move, because it is easy to miss. Meno said 'honourable'; Socrates immediately asks whether desiring the honourable is desiring 'the good', and from then on argues about good and evil in the sense of what benefits or harms the person who has it. With that substitution in place the argument runs smoothly. Some people want bad things thinking they are good; those people really want good things and are merely mistaken. Others, Meno says, want bad things knowing they are harmful. But to be harmed is to be miserable, and nobody wants to be miserable. So nobody wants evil. I have never been able to decide whether this is profound or a sleight of hand. It is true that people rarely choose something under the description 'bad for me'. It also seems plainly true that people light the next cigarette knowing. Socrates' position leaves no room for that, and Meno, who has presumably met a self-destructive person, gives in rather fast. What matters for the rest of the dialogue is the consequence: if everyone wants the good, then what separates good people from bad cannot be what they want. It must be something they know or can do. Keep that; it comes back with force.

The second half, the 'power of attaining' goods, goes down more easily. Meno's goods turn out to be gold, silver and office, and Socrates cannot resist a jab at this 'hereditary friend of the great king', meaning the king of Persia. Must the gold be got justly? Of course, says Meno. Then getting it is no more virtuous than going without it, and all the work in the definition is being done by 'justly'. And justice, Meno has already said, is a part of virtue. So virtue has been defined as acting with a part of virtue, which is the swarm a third time, now 'frittered away into little pieces'.

Socrates' complaint that Meno 'mocks' him is comic, but the rule he invokes is the one Meno himself insisted on in [[me2]]: no defining in terms not yet understood. Meno is caught by his own objection, and he knows it. Three answers, three failures, and each time Socrates ends by asking for what 'you and your friend Gorgias' say. The borrowed stock is exhausted.

annotations.quote: Virtue is the desire of things honourable and the power of attaining them.
annotations.note: Meno's third definition is a quotation, from a poet nobody can now identify. That is his habit: asked what he thinks, he recites. It is also the first definition with any shape to it, a wanting plus an ability, and Socrates pays it the respect of taking each half seriously.

annotations.quote: Do not all men, my dear sir, desire good?
annotations.note: The Socratic thesis arrives as a rhetorical question. Note the quiet switch just before it, from Meno's 'honourable' to Socrates' 'good'. Those are not obviously the same thing, and the argument depends on treating them as if they were.

annotations.quote: they desire what they suppose to be goods although they are really evils
annotations.note: The first half of the case, and the persuasive half. Someone who wants a harmful thing because he thinks it will benefit him is aiming at benefit; the error is in his beliefs, not his desires. This turns wickedness into a kind of mistake, which is where Socrates wants it.

annotations.quote: for what is misery but the desire and possession of evil?
annotations.note: The clincher, and I think the weakest link. It works only if 'evil' means 'what makes its possessor wretched', so that wanting evil just is wanting to be wretched. Meno never asks whether a man might want what is bad for others, or want something badly enough not to care.

annotations.quote: according to Meno, who is the hereditary friend of the great king, virtue is the power of getting silver and gold
annotations.note: The 'great king' is the king of Persia, and Meno's family had ties of guest-friendship with him. Socrates states the definition back with the full title attached, so that it sounds like what it is: a rich man's idea of excellence.

annotations.quote: And so, Meno, this is the way in which you mock me.
annotations.note: Mock indignation. Socrates asked for virtue 'whole and unbroken' and has been handed fragments again. The pretence that Meno is the one playing games is funny, and it also keeps the tone friendly at the exact moment Meno is being shown he has nothing left.

annotations.quote: for can any one who does not know virtue know a part of virtue?
annotations.note: The priority-of-definition rule from the opening, now with teeth. If you cannot know a part without knowing the whole, every one of Meno's answers was illegitimate from the start. It is a very strong demand, and it is about to provoke a very strong objection.

annotations.quote: What, according to you and your friend Gorgias, is the definition of virtue?
annotations.note: The fourth time of asking, in nearly the same words as the first. The conversation has gone in a circle and Socrates makes the circle audible. Meno's next speech is not a definition.

links.why: The rule Socrates uses to finish off this definition, no explaining by the unexplained, is the one Meno demanded during the lesson on figure.
The claim that everyone desires the good is picked up again when Socrates argues that what makes anything beneficial is wisdom.
Meno's response to this third failure is the torpedo-fish speech.

me4.essay:
Here the dialogue changes key. Up to now it has looked like one of the short Socratic conversations that end in honest failure, the pattern of the [[eu1|Euthyphro]]. Meno, cornered, does what Euthyphro never does: he describes what it feels like. Socrates is a 'torpedo fish', the electric ray that numbs whatever touches it (the weapon is named after the fish, not the other way round), and Meno's 'soul and tongue are really torpid'. He has made 'an infinite variety of speeches about virtue', and very good ones he thought, and now cannot say what it is. I find this the most sympathetic Meno gets. He also slips in a warning that reads differently to anyone who has come here from the [[ap1|Apology]]: in any other city, a man who did this would be arrested as a sorcerer.

Socrates' reply is the important correction. The ray is not numb itself. 'I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself.' He is not withholding an answer. Then he proposes they search together, and Meno produces the objection that has kept the dialogue famous. How do you look for something when you do not know what it is? What would you aim at? And if you stumbled on it, how would you recognise it? Socrates calls this 'tiresome' and restates it as a neat dilemma, but I think Meno's own version, particularly the last question, is sharper than the restatement, and it is a genuine problem, not a debater's trick. Anyone who has tried to work out what they actually think about something knows the oddity of recognising the right answer on arrival.

The response is not an argument. It is a story heard from 'priests and priestesses' and from Pindar: the soul is immortal, has been born many times, has seen everything, and so what we call learning is 'but recollection'. I notice how carefully Socrates holds this at arm's length. He has heard it; he asks Meno to 'see whether their words are true'. And the reason he gives for preferring it to the paradox is not that it is proven but that it is better for us: the paradox 'will make us idle', the other saying 'active and inquisitive'. That is a remarkable thing for a philosopher to say out loud, and he will say it again, more firmly, when the demonstration is done.

Meno then asks to be taught that there is no teaching, and gets called a rogue for the second time. He says it was only habit. I believe him.

annotations.quote: very like the flat torpedo fish, who torpifies those who come near him and touch him
annotations.note: 'Torpedo' is the old name for the electric ray, and 'torpifies' is Jowett stretching English to keep the pun on numbness. The gibe at Socrates' 'appearance' is real too: by all accounts he was broad-faced and snub-nosed. Meno is being rude and accurate at once.

annotations.quote: though I have been delivered of an infinite variety of speeches about virtue before now
annotations.note: The confession that makes the scene. Meno has lectured on virtue many times, to audiences, and thought he did it well. Fluency turned out not to be knowledge, and he has just felt the difference in his own mouth.

annotations.quote: you would be cast into prison as a magician
annotations.note: Meant as a joke, and a chilling one. Meno says Socrates is wise not to travel, since other cities would not put up with him. A reader who knows the [[ap1|Apology]] knows how far Athens' own patience extends.

annotations.quote: I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself
annotations.note: Socrates accepts the comparison on one condition: that the ray numbs itself too. This is the difference between him and a debater who ties people in knots for sport. He is not hiding the answer; he is in the same water.

annotations.quote: And if you find what you want, how will you ever know that this is the thing which you did not know?
annotations.note: The sharpest of Meno's three questions, and the one Socrates leaves out when he restates the puzzle. It is the problem of recognition: without already knowing the answer, by what mark would you tell it from a plausible impostor? Meno may have picked the argument up second-hand, but it is a real one.

annotations.quote: I have heard from certain wise men and women who spoke of things divine
annotations.note: Notice the sourcing. The answer to the paradox comes as hearsay from priests, priestesses and poets, and Socrates breaks off mid-sentence so that Meno has to ask twice. It is theatre, and it also marks what follows as something other than his usual step-by-step argument.

annotations.quote: for all enquiry and all learning is but recollection
annotations.note: The doctrine in eight words. If the soul has seen everything already, then finding out is remembering, and Meno's puzzle dissolves: you can recognise the answer because you have met it before. Whether one believes the premise is another matter, and Socrates seems aware of that.

annotations.quote: for it will make us idle; and is sweet only to the sluggard
annotations.note: The stated reason for rejecting the paradox is its effect on character, not a flaw in its logic. Socrates is choosing between two beliefs partly by asking which one makes a better inquirer of the person who holds it. Hold on to this; he comes back to it.

annotations.quote: I only asked the question from habit
annotations.note: Meno has just asked Socrates to 'teach' him that nothing is taught. Socrates suspects a trap; Meno pleads habit, and I think the plea is true and more damaging than a trap would have been. Asking to be told is simply what he does.

links.why: Meno's joke about being jailed as a magician, and Socrates' claim to be perplexed himself, both read differently beside his own account of why people came to hate him.
That conversation follows the same pattern of failed definitions but stops where this one turns and begins again.
The story told here on the authority of priests and poets is put to a practical test on one of Meno's slaves.

me5.essay:
This is the most famous scene in the dialogue and one of the few places in Plato where you should stop reading and pick up a pencil. Socrates is drawing in the sand, and every 'this line' and 'this space' points at something we cannot see. Draw a square two feet on a side, so four square feet in area. The question put to the boy is: how long is the side of a square with twice the area, eight?

It goes in three stages, and Socrates stops after each to talk to Meno over the boy's head. First, false confidence. 'Clearly, Socrates, it will be double.' Double the side and you get a square of sixteen, four times too big. The boy tries three, the obvious number between two and four, and gets nine. Second, perplexity: 'Indeed, Socrates, I do not know.' Third, Socrates draws four of the small squares together, cuts each in half with a line from corner to corner, and the four diagonals enclose a tilted square made of four halves, which is to say eight. The side wanted is the diagonal.

The middle stage is the one I would underline. Socrates turns to Meno and asks whether the boy is worse off for having been numbed, using Meno's own image back at him: 'the torpedo's shock'. Before, the boy would have told 'all the world again and again' that double area needs double side. Now he knows he does not know, and wants to. Meno agrees readily that this is an improvement, and seems not to notice he is agreeing about himself. He too made many confident speeches; he too was stopped. The geometry lesson is, among other things, a mirror held up to the previous hour, and a defence of what looked like mere demolition in [[me3]].

There is also a small piece of cunning in the choice of problem. The answer cannot be said as a number. The side of the eight-foot square is not two, not three, not any fraction of feet a boy could name, and Socrates quietly allows for this: 'if you would rather not reckon, try and show me the line.' The truth can be pointed at before it can be stated. I think that is meant to carry over to virtue, which Meno also cannot state.

Now the obvious objection, which every reader makes and should. Socrates says, repeatedly, that he is 'not teaching the boy anything, but only asking him questions.' But the questions are as leading as questions can be, and it is Socrates, not the boy, who draws the diagonal. The boy's part in the final stage is mostly 'Yes.' Is this recollection or dictation? My own view is that the objection is half right. Socrates certainly supplies the idea. What he cannot supply is the seeing. At each step the boy has to look and judge for himself whether four is twice two, whether the line halves the square, and he could say no; indeed twice he gives wrong answers that are honestly his own, and once says 'I do not understand.' Nobody is asking him to take anything on authority, which is how he would have to take the date of a battle. That difference, between being told and seeing that it must be so, is real, and it is what the scene establishes. Whether it requires a soul that existed before birth is another matter.

Socrates himself seems to know this. Look at how modest the claims become when he sums up. The boy does not yet have knowledge, only true notions 'stirred up in him, as in a dream'; he would need to be asked again, many times and in different ways, before he knew. Hold on to that distinction between a true notion and knowledge; the dialogue is not finished with it. The argument to immortality then goes by at a speed that would not survive a hostile witness: he was never taught, so he always had it, so the soul always existed. Meno, who is not a hostile witness, says 'Obviously.' The same doctrine is put under heavier pressure in the [[pha1|Phaedo]].

And then the sentence I think is the heart of the whole dialogue. 'Some things I have said of which I am not altogether confident.' What he will fight for 'in word and deed' is not reincarnation. It is that we will be 'better and braver and less helpless' if we believe inquiry is worth the trouble than if we take the lazy view that there is no finding out. The myth is offered as scaffolding for a commitment, and the commitment is the thing. I find that more moving than the proof, and more honest.

One last thing nobody in the scene remarks on. The person in whom the eternal truths of geometry are shown to reside is a nameless household slave, summoned with 'Come hither, boy' and never thanked. Whatever Plato intended, the demonstration says that the capacity to see what is true has nothing to do with rank. Meno, owner of 'numerous attendants', draws no conclusion.

annotations.quote: He is Greek, and speaks Greek, does he not?
annotations.note: The only qualification Socrates asks for. No schooling, no cleverness, just a shared language to ask questions in. Meno's answer, that the boy was born in the house, will matter later as evidence: Meno can vouch that nobody ever taught him geometry.

annotations.quote: Clearly, Socrates, it will be double.
annotations.note: The natural mistake, and the word to notice is 'Clearly'. The boy is not guessing timidly; he is sure. It is the geometrical twin of Meno's opening 'There will be no difficulty, Socrates' back in [[me1]].

annotations.quote: Very good; I like to hear you say what you think.
annotations.note: The boy has just ventured 'I think so', and Socrates praises the hedge. It is a small kindness and a statement of method. The answers must be the boy's own opinions or the demonstration proves nothing.

annotations.quote: Indeed, Socrates, I do not know.
annotations.note: The turning point of the lesson, and the same place Meno reached when he compared Socrates to a stingray. The difference is in the tone. The boy says it without resentment and without worrying what anyone will think of him.

annotations.quote: Is he not better off in knowing his ignorance?
annotations.note: The question is about the boy and aimed at his master. Meno answers 'I think that he is' and so, without noticing, withdraws his complaint about being numbed. Socrates lets him not notice.

annotations.quote: he would have been ready to tell all the world again and again that the double space should have a double side
annotations.note: A precise echo of Meno's 'infinite variety of speeches about virtue' delivered 'to many persons'. The boy lecturing the world on his wrong answer is a caricature of Meno on the platform. I doubt Meno hears it.

annotations.quote: And does not this line, reaching from corner to corner, bisect each of these spaces?
annotations.note: Here is where the 'only asking' claim is most strained. The diagonal is Socrates' idea, drawn by Socrates' hand; the boy would not have found it alone in an afternoon. What the boy contributes is the recognition, once it is drawn, that it works.

annotations.quote: these notions have just been stirred up in him, as in a dream
annotations.note: A careful and easily missed qualification. The boy has got the right answer but does not yet know it; his true notions are dreamlike, and only repeated questioning 'in different forms' would turn them into knowledge. This gap between having the truth and knowing it comes back at the end of the dialogue.

annotations.quote: Some things I have said of which I am not altogether confident.
annotations.note: Socrates grades his own argument. He will not go to the wall for the pre-existing soul. What he will fight for is the practical belief that searching makes us 'better and braver and less helpless' than giving up. I take this as the sentence the scene exists to earn.

links.why: The demonstration is offered as proof of the recollection story told there, and as Socrates' answer to the torpedo-fish complaint.
The boy's dreamlike 'true notions' that are not yet knowledge become the distinction on which the whole dialogue ends.
Recollection and the soul's existence before birth are taken up again there, with more at stake and tougher questioners.

me6.essay:
Meno has just agreed, warmly, that one should inquire into what one does not know, and into 'the nature of virtue' in particular. His very next sentence: 'And yet I would much rather return to my original question.' It is funny and a little dispiriting. The slave boy made progress in ten minutes; his owner is exactly where he started. Socrates gives way with a barbed remark about Meno controlling everyone except himself, 'such being your notion of freedom', and then does something clever: he finds a way to work on Meno's question that still smuggles in his own.

The device is borrowed from geometers, and Jowett's rendering of the example, the triangle to be inscribed in a circle, is frankly impenetrable; his own parenthetical alternatives show he was not sure what the Greek meant, and scholars still argue. It can be skipped without loss. The idea is simple. When you cannot answer a question directly, find a condition on which it turns: if such-and-such holds, the answer is yes; if not, no. Here: if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it can be taught; if not, not. The question 'is it teachable?' has been turned into 'is it knowledge?', which is a question about what virtue is. Socrates has given way and lost nothing.

The argument that virtue is knowledge is the positive centre of the dialogue, and it is a good one. Virtue is good, so always beneficial. But nearly everything we call good, health, wealth, strength, can hurt as well as help, depending on how it is used. Even qualities of character: courage without sense is 'only a sort of confidence', and gets people killed. The one thing that makes all the others turn out well is the wisdom that directs them. Remember the conclusion in [[me3]] that everyone wants the good; put it beside this and you have the full Socratic picture, in which people go wrong only by not knowing how to get what they want.

Notice a slip of the tongue, or what Socrates passes off as one: knowledge is 'taught', or 'as we were just now saying, remembered', and there is 'no use in disputing about the name.' But a great deal hangs on the name. If learning is recollection, 'taught' cannot mean what Meno means by it.

And then, with the conclusion in hand, Socrates turns on it. A sound principle should hold 'not only just now, but always.' If virtue were teachable there would be teachers and pupils. Where are they? It is an appeal to the facts, and a strange thing to set against an argument; but it is what the next pages are about.

annotations.quote: And yet I would much rather return to my original question
annotations.note: One breath after agreeing to inquire into what virtue is, Meno asks again how it is acquired. Nothing in the last hour has changed what he wants, which is a usable answer to take home. I find it one of the most lifelike moments in Plato.

annotations.quote: you think only of controlling me who am your slave, and never of controlling yourself
annotations.note: The flirtatious 'tyrannical' of [[me2]] with the charm taken off. Socrates calls himself Meno's slave minutes after a real slave has been sent away, and says that giving orders to others while ungoverned oneself is Meno's 'notion of freedom'. It is the hardest thing he says to him.

annotations.quote: or rather, does not every one see that knowledge alone is taught?
annotations.note: The premise the whole section rests on, slipped in as something 'every one' sees. Just before it Socrates waves away the difference between 'taught' and 'remembered' as a quarrel about names. After the slave boy, that difference is surely not nothing.

annotations.quote: courage wanting prudence, which is only a sort of confidence
annotations.note: A striking demotion. Courage, one of the great virtues on Meno's list, is here treated as raw material that can harm its owner unless sense directs it. The argument needs every good except wisdom to be capable of going wrong, and this is the hardest case made to look easy.

annotations.quote: All other things hang upon the soul, and the things of the soul herself hang upon wisdom
annotations.note: The argument compressed into a chain: outward goods depend on how the soul uses them, and the soul's own qualities depend on wisdom. Jowett's 'hang upon' is good, plain English for dependence. It is as close as the dialogue comes to saying what virtue is.

annotations.quote: we should have kept them in the citadel out of the way of harm, and set a stamp upon them far rather than upon a piece of gold
annotations.note: A playful picture: if goodness were inborn, the city would identify its gifted children early and lock them in the treasury on the Acropolis, sealed like bullion. Since nobody does this, nobody believes virtue comes by nature. That disposes of one of Meno's three options in a single sentence.

annotations.quote: a principle which has any soundness should stand firm not only just now, but always
annotations.note: Socrates undermines his own result the moment Meno is happy with it. The standard he sets, that a real conclusion must stay put, sounds like fussiness here. Remember the wording; staying put turns out to be the point.

annotations.quote: why are you so slow of heart to believe that knowledge is virtue?
annotations.note: 'Slow of heart to believe' is a phrase from the King James Bible, and Jowett, a clergyman, drops it in without blinking. It gives Meno a preacherly impatience he does not quite have in Greek. He has also, I notice, got the thesis back to front.

links.why: The claim there that no one desires evil supplies the other half of this section's argument that virtue is a kind of wisdom.
Meno's retreat to his first question is best read straight after the slave boy's progress, and the 'taught or remembered' slip depends on it.
The doubt raised in the closing lines, that there seem to be no teachers of virtue, is put to a prominent Athenian.

me7.essay:
Anytus is simply 'sitting by us', and Socrates draws him in with elaborate courtesy. For anyone who has read the [[ap1|Apology]] the name lands like a dropped plate: this is one of the three men who brought Socrates to trial, and the one with real political weight. Plato wrote this scene knowing that, for readers who knew it, and every polite phrase in it is lit from behind.

For medicine you go to doctors, for shoes to cobblers, to people who profess the craft and charge for it. Who professes to teach virtue for a fee? The Sophists. Anytus explodes: 'By Heracles, Socrates, forbear!' They are a pest, they corrupt whoever goes near them. Has he ever met one? No, and he does not wish to. 'I am sure that I know what manner of men these are, whether I am acquainted with them or not.' Socrates replies that he must be a diviner. He is not really defending the Sophists here. What he is exposing is a man who is certain without having looked, which is the condition the slave boy was cured of in [[me5]]. And 'corrupt' is the very word of the charge against Socrates. Anytus hates the Sophists, and does not seem a man likely to distinguish Socrates from them.

Anytus' own answer is that any Athenian gentleman will do. So Socrates goes through the gentlemen. Themistocles, Aristides, Pericles, Thucydides (the statesman, not the historian): each paid for his sons to have the best training money could buy, in riding, music, wrestling, and each son turned out ordinary. If these men could have passed on what made them great, would they have stopped at javelin tricks on horseback? I think this is a much weaker argument than Socrates makes it sound. Sons of great men are a small and peculiar sample, and failing to teach something is not proof it cannot be taught. But as a thing to say to Anytus' face it is devastating, because Anytus counts himself among these gentlemen, and he hears his whole class being told it has nothing to hand on.

His reply is a threat, barely dressed: it is easier in Athens to do men harm than good, 'as I believe that you know.' After that he says nothing more. Socrates' comment is extraordinary in its calm. Some day Anytus will learn what defamation really is, 'and if he ever does, he will forgive me.'
