Then back to Meno, quickly. The gentlemen of Thessaly cannot agree whether virtue is teachable; Gorgias laughs at those who promise it; even the poet Theognis says both things. No agreed teachers, so no teaching. Meno accepts each step, though not happily.

annotations.quote: Here at the moment when he is wanted we fortunately have sitting by us Anytus
annotations.note: The entrance is almost comically convenient, and 'fortunately' is not the word a reader of the [[ap1|Apology]] would choose. The praise that follows, of his self-made father and his election to high office, is so smooth that it is hard to tell where courtesy ends and irony begins. I suspect that is deliberate.

annotations.quote: By Heracles, Socrates, forbear!
annotations.note: Jowett's 'forbear!' is a Victorian gentleman's splutter, and it suits Anytus well. The mere word 'Sophists' sets him off. The violence of the reaction, before any argument has been made, tells you what kind of conversation this is going to be.

annotations.quote: during more than forty years, Protagoras was corrupting all Hellas
annotations.note: Socrates' argument is commercial: a cobbler who ruined shoes would be found out in a month, so how did Protagoras ruin young men for forty years and die with his reputation intact? Socrates is no friend of the Sophists, but he will not let a charge of corrupting the young stand on indignation alone.

annotations.quote: I am sure that I know what manner of men these are, whether I am acquainted with them or not
annotations.note: Prejudice stated as a principle. Anytus has just admitted he has never met a Sophist and does not wish to. Set this beside the slave boy's 'I do not know' and Meno's numbness: Anytus is the one character in the dialogue whom the torpedo cannot touch.

annotations.quote: Any Athenian gentleman, taken at random, if he will mind him, will do far more good to him than the Sophists.
annotations.note: 'Gentleman' is Jowett's rendering of a Greek phrase meaning, roughly, the fine and good: the respectable citizen class. Anytus' theory of moral education is that decent people rub off on you. It is not a stupid view, and Socrates' reply attacks it only at its strongest-looking point, the famous fathers.

annotations.quote: had him taught to stand upright on horseback and hurl a javelin
annotations.note: The detail is wonderfully chosen. The son of the man who saved Greece at Salamis is remembered as a trick rider. Whatever Themistocles had, it was evidently not something a hired master could drill into a boy.

annotations.quote: if you will take my advice, I would recommend you to be careful
annotations.note: The mask comes off. This is advice in the sense that a hand on the shoulder is advice, and the sentence that follows, about how easy it is to do a man harm in Athens, removes any doubt. In a book that also contains the trial, it is the most ominous line in the dialogue.

annotations.quote: But some day he will know what is the meaning of defamation, and if he ever does, he will forgive me.
annotations.note: Socrates answers a threat with something close to pity. Anytus thinks he has been slandered; Socrates says he does not yet know what slander is. I read it as saying that a man who understood the thing would have no anger left, which is the 'no one does wrong knowingly' of [[me3]] applied to an enemy.

annotations.quote: Gorgias is never heard promising to teach virtue: and when he hears others promising he only laughs at them
annotations.note: A small surprise held back until now. Meno's own master, whose views on virtue Socrates has been asking for since the first page, never claimed to teach it at all, only to make men good speakers. Meno 'often wonders' at this, and it does not seem to have troubled him further.

links.why: Anytus appears there as an accuser, and Socrates explains the resentment of the politicians and craftsmen that this scene shows being born.
Anytus' certainty about people he has never met is the opposite of the slave boy's honest 'I do not know'.
The great statesmen who could not teach their sons are explained there, in a way Anytus would not enjoy.

me8.essay:
Meno will not swallow the conclusion, and to his credit. If virtue cannot be taught, where do good men come from? 'I cannot believe, Socrates, that there are no good men.' It is the second time he has dug his heels in against an argument on behalf of plain experience, and the second time he is onto something. Socrates' answer is to go back and find the mistake, and he finds it in the argument of [[me6]] that looked so strong: they assumed that only knowledge can guide action well.

The example is as homely as the correction is important. A man who has walked the road to Larisa can lead you there. So can a man who has never been but happens to have the right idea of the way. As long as his opinion is true, you arrive just the same. (Larisa is in Thessaly; Socrates has picked the road to Meno's own country, which I take as a small courtesy and a small joke.) So true opinion is 'as good a guide to correct action as knowledge.' Meno's first response is the sensible one: the man who knows will always be right, the other only sometimes. Socrates pounces: how can someone with a right opinion be wrong, so long as he has it? Meno gives in, and then asks the question that makes this section the richest in the dialogue. If they work equally well, why do we prize knowledge more? Why are they even different?

Philosophers are still answering that. Socrates' answer is an image: the statues of Daedalus, so lifelike that they 'play truant and run away' unless tied down. He reached for the same statues in the [[eu1|Euthyphro]], where it was statements that would not stay put. A true opinion is a fine thing while it stays, but it does not stay. It wanders off under pressure, under persuasion, when circumstances change. What ties it down is what Jowett calls, a little stiffly, 'the tie of the cause': working out why the thing is so. An opinion fastened to its reasons becomes knowledge and becomes stable. So Meno's first instinct was right after all. The difference shows not on the single journey but over time; the man with the mere opinion is the one a persuasive stranger can talk into the wrong turning.

And then Socrates adds, almost in passing, that this fastening 'is recollection, as you and I have agreed to call it.' Here the whole dialogue clicks together. The slave boy at the end of [[me5]] had true notions, stirred up 'as in a dream', which would become knowledge only with repeated questioning. That was the gap between opinion and knowledge, shown before it was named. And Meno at the start had a head full of things Gorgias had told him, some of them perhaps true, none of them tied down, all of which walked off the moment Socrates touched them. I think the Daedalus passage is the real answer to the torpedo complaint of [[me4]]. Being numbed is what it feels like to find that your opinions were never fastened.

One sentence deserves to be read twice. Socrates, who has spent the whole conversation disclaiming knowledge, says: 'There are not many things which I profess to know, but this is most certainly one of them.' That knowledge differs from true opinion is on the very short list. Set that beside his lack of confidence about reincarnation, and you can see what he actually stands on.

The official conclusion follows quickly, and I do not think it should be taken at face value. Since virtue is evidently not taught, it is not knowledge; so the great statesmen steered by true opinion, like diviners and prophets who 'say many things truly, but they know not what they say'; so their virtue came by divine gift. Jowett's 'gift of God' and 'instinct given by God' make this sound more pious and more Christian than the Greek, which speaks of a divine allotment, something nearer to luck. And the compliment is double-edged. 'Divine' here means inspired and uncomprehending. In the [[ap1|Apology]] Socrates says much the same about the poets, and it was not praise. A Themistocles who got it right without knowing why is a man with untethered statues, which is precisely why he could pass nothing on to his son. Meno, enjoying himself, notes that Anytus would not like the word.

Then a door is left open. All this holds 'unless' there should be a statesman who could make another like himself; such a man would be like Tiresias among the dead, the only one with his wits, 'a reality among shadows'. Plato does not say who that might be. He does not need to.

And the last speech takes it all back anyway. We will 'never know the certain truth' about how virtue comes until we ask what it is, which is where Socrates wanted to start and Meno would not. The dialogue ends on its own first page, with one difference: we now know what kind of thing an answer would have to be. Socrates leaves, asking Meno to soothe Anytus, for the good of Athens. He was not soothed.

annotations.quote: But I cannot believe, Socrates, that there are no good men
annotations.note: Meno refuses to follow an argument off a cliff. If the reasoning says there is no way for good men to come about, and yet there are good men, the reasoning has gone wrong somewhere. It is the instinct that saves the conversation, and Socrates rewards it by reopening the case.

annotations.quote: If a man knew the way to Larisa, or anywhere else, and went to the place and led others thither
annotations.note: The most famous example in the dialogue, and deliberately ordinary. Larisa is the Thessalian city Socrates named on the first page, home of Meno's friends. Knowing here means having been there; the contrast is with someone who merely has the right directions.

annotations.quote: he who has knowledge will always be right; but he who has right opinion will sometimes be right, and sometimes not
annotations.note: Meno's objection, which Socrates bats away on a technicality: while the opinion is right, it is right. But Meno is groping at the correct point, that opinion is unreliable over time, and within a page Socrates' own answer will say exactly that in better words.

annotations.quote: if they are not fastened they will play truant and run away
annotations.note: Daedalus was the legendary craftsman whose statues were said to be so lifelike they moved. 'Play truant' is a schoolroom phrase, Jowett's touch, and it makes the statues sound like naughty boys. The image is comic on purpose: a truth you cannot keep hold of is a slightly ridiculous possession.

annotations.quote: they are not of much value until they are fastened by the tie of the cause
annotations.note: The key phrase, in cramped English. The Greek means something like reasoning out the explanation: an opinion becomes knowledge when you can say why it is true. Jowett's 'tie' keeps the tethering image, at some cost to clarity. This is the nearest thing to a definition of knowledge the dialogue offers.

annotations.quote: There are not many things which I profess to know, but this is most certainly one of them.
annotations.note: A rare flat claim to knowledge from the man who claims to know nothing. Even the Daedalus image he calls conjecture; that knowledge and true opinion differ, he knows. If you want to find the floor Socrates is standing on, it is here.

annotations.quote: which is in politics what divination is in religion
annotations.note: The great statesmen of Athens are compared to soothsayers: often right, never able to say why. It is delivered as an explanation of their success and works as a demolition of their authority. Recall who has just been sitting there defending them.

annotations.quote: he alone has understanding; but the rest are flitting shades
annotations.note: A line from the Odyssey about the prophet Tiresias, the one ghost in the underworld who kept his mind. Socrates applies it to a hypothetical statesman who could actually teach virtue, because he knew what it was. The dialogue leaves the chair empty and lets the reader think of a candidate.

annotations.quote: But we shall never know the certain truth until, before asking how virtue is given, we enquire into the actual nature of virtue.
annotations.note: The last word undoes the conclusion just reached. 'Gift of God' was the answer to Meno's question, pursued in Meno's order, and Socrates marks it as provisional for exactly that reason. The dialogue closes by pointing back to the question Meno kept refusing in [[me1]].

links.why: The slave boy's 'true notions' that were not yet knowledge are the demonstration of the distinction drawn here.
The assumption being corrected, that only knowledge guides action rightly, was made in the argument from hypothesis.
The runaway statues of Daedalus first appear there, in a conversation whose conclusions would not stay where they were put.
Socrates' account of poets and politicians who say fine things without understanding them shows what 'divine' is worth as a compliment.

pha1.essay:
Plato opens the death of Socrates at two removes. We are not in the prison but in Phlius, a small town in the Peloponnese, some unstated time afterwards, and a man who was there is being questioned by a man who was not. I think the distance is the point. Echecrates knows the bare fact, 'that he died by taking poison, but no one knew anything more', and what he wants is exactly what a reader wants: what was said, who was there, how he bore it. Twice he asks Phaedo to be 'as exact as you can'. Everything that follows comes to us as testimony, remembered and retold, which is a quiet irony in a dialogue that is about to argue that all learning is remembering.

The delay between sentence and death is explained by an 'accident': the sacred ship to Delos was garlanded the day before the trial, and Athens does not execute while it is away. Readers who have come from [[cr1|the Crito]] have already waited for that ship. Here it is given its story, Theseus and the fourteen youths saved from Crete, and I do not think Plato tells it idly. A man is about to lead a band of young companions through a labyrinth of argument with a monster at the centre, the fear of death; and Apollo, the god of the voyage, will be claimed by Socrates as his own master before the day is out.

Then Phaedo's report of his own feelings, which is the truest thing in these pages. He did not pity Socrates; he could not feel the usual pleasure of philosophy either; 'we were laughing and weeping by turns'. That mixed state is the key signature of the whole dialogue, and Socrates' first words in it are a little theory of the same mixture. Freed from the fetters, rubbing his leg, he observes that pleasure and pain are like two bodies 'joined by a single head'. It is a charming, offhand remark, and it is also the first appearance of the day's great subject: opposites, and how one comes out of the other.

Notice too who is and is not in the room. Xanthippe is sent home with a curtness I find hard to like. And 'Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill': the author signs his masterpiece by marking himself absent, which I take as fair warning that this is not a transcript.

annotations.quote: for no Phliasian ever goes to Athens now
annotations.note: The news has to travel. Phlius was a centre of Pythagorean thinking, a school that believed in the soul's rebirth, so Phaedo is telling this story to an audience already half inclined to its conclusion. It is worth remembering later, when the objections come, that the listeners want Socrates to win.

annotations.quote: the stern of the ship which the Athenians send to Delos happened to have been crowned on the day before he was tried
annotations.note: Phaedo calls it an accident, but the dialogue will not treat it as one. The pause belongs to Apollo, and Socrates spends it, as we are about to learn, writing a hymn to Apollo. This is the same ship whose return Crito dreads in [[cr1]].

annotations.quote: To be reminded of Socrates is always the greatest delight to me
annotations.note: Jowett's 'reminded' is a happy choice. Recollection will be one of the main proofs of the soul's survival, and here, before any argument, is the plain human version: a dead man kept present by being recalled.

annotations.quote: we were laughing and weeping by turns, especially the excitable Apollodorus
annotations.note: Phaedo is describing a feeling he has no name for, pleasure with 'a strange admixture of pain'. Hold on to it. A minute later Socrates, rubbing his leg, will say the same thing about pleasure and pain in general.

annotations.quote: Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill.
annotations.note: One of only a handful of places where Plato names himself in his own work, and he does it to say he was not there. The 'if I am not mistaken' is a nice touch of deniability. Whatever we are about to read, its author is telling us he did not witness it.

annotations.quote: Crito, let some one take her home.
annotations.note: The hardest line in the opening. Xanthippe has said nothing foolish; what she says is simply true, that this is the last conversation. But grief is exactly what the day's talk is meant to master, and she is removed so that it can begin. The women return briefly near the end of [[phb1]], and are sent away again.

annotations.quote: their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head
annotations.note: A fable Aesop never wrote, improvised on the spot from a sore leg. It sounds like small talk, but the idea that opposites follow one another by necessity becomes the first formal argument for immortality in [[pha4]].

links.why: The Crito opens with the news that this same ship is nearly home; here we learn why it mattered and what its return costs.
The trial Echecrates has only heard about at second hand, and the speech this dialogue will set out to better.
The idle remark about pleasure following pain grows into the argument that the living come from the dead.

pha2.essay:
A stretch of what looks like preliminaries, and I would not skip a line of it. Cebes asks, on behalf of the poet Evenus, why Socrates has taken to verse in prison. The answer is one of the most disarming things he ever says. A dream has told him all his life to 'make music'; he always took it to mean philosophy, 'the noblest and best of music', cheering him on as spectators cheer a runner who is already running. Now, with days in hand, he is no longer sure, and so he hedges: a hymn to Apollo, some Aesop in metre. The man who told his jury in [[ap1|the Apology]] that he knew nothing worth knowing is still, on his last morning, checking whether he misread his own vocation. And he is funny about his limits: a poet must invent stories, 'and that I have no invention'. This from the character who will be telling a tremendous story about the afterlife before sunset.

The message to Evenus, to follow him quickly, lets the real subject in by a side door. A philosopher will be willing to die, but must not kill himself. Cebes sees at once that this looks like a contradiction, and Socrates' explanation is, by his own admission, borrowed and dim: 'a doctrine whispered in secret' that we are in a kind of prison (the Greek word behind Jowett's 'prisoner' can also mean a guard-post, a place one is stationed), and the plainer thought that we are the gods' property, like an ox that has no business putting itself 'out of the way'. I find the cattle argument thin. It says whom suicide wrongs, on a premise few would now grant, and nothing about why death should be welcome.

Cebes makes it worse, and this is the best moment in the section. If the gods are such good masters, a wise man should hate to leave their service; so 'the wise man should sorrow and the fool rejoice' at dying. Socrates is delighted with him. He does not answer directly; he accepts the form of the charge. 'I must try to make a more successful defence before you than I did when before the judges.' So the rest of the Phaedo is a second Apology, argued before friends instead of five hundred strangers, with the odd difference that this jury wants to acquit him and cannot quite manage it. Before it starts, Crito relays the executioner's advice not to talk so much. The reply is the whole man.

annotations.quote: the dream might have meant music in the popular sense of the word
annotations.note: After seventy years he allows that he may have misunderstood his calling, and takes out insurance. I find this more persuasive of his sincerity than any of the confident passages: he treats a dream the way he treats an argument, as something that might mean other than he assumed.

annotations.quote: should not only put together words, but should invent stories, and that I have no invention
annotations.note: A fair joke at his own expense, and at Plato's. Socrates has just invented a fable about pleasure and pain, and will end the day with a long myth of the earth and the underworld. The writer who gives him 'no invention' is the most inventive prose artist in Greek.

annotations.quote: Here he changed his position, and put his legs off the couch on to the ground
annotations.note: Phaedo remembers the posture. Until now Socrates has been half reclining and chatting; with his feet on the floor he is at work. Plato marks the start of the serious conversation with a movement of the body, in a dialogue that is about to speak very harshly of the body.

annotations.quote: laughing gently and speaking in his native Boeotian
annotations.note: A lovely small detail. Cebes is a foreigner from Thebes, and when he is caught off guard he slips into dialect, something like a visitor lapsing into broad Scots. These are real young men, and they laugh a good deal for people at a deathbed.

annotations.quote: There is a doctrine whispered in secret that man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away
annotations.note: Said by a man sitting in an actual prison who was offered an actual open door and refused it; see [[cr1]]. Socrates confesses he does not quite understand the doctrine, which is unusual candour about a premise he is about to rely on.

annotations.quote: for upon this view the wise man should sorrow and the fool rejoice at passing out of life
annotations.note: Cebes turns Socrates' own premise against him in four sentences. If our masters here are good, leaving them is a loss. This is the objection that forces the whole defence, and it is never answered on its own terms; Socrates replies only that he expects equally good masters elsewhere.

annotations.quote: Then I must try to make a more successful defence before you than I did when before the judges.
annotations.note: The dialogue names its own genre. He lost the first trial; this is the retrial, and the charge is no longer corrupting the young but being too willing to leave them. The courtroom language keeps returning, down to 'O my judges' a page later.

annotations.quote: let him mind his business and be prepared to give the poison twice or even thrice if necessary
annotations.note: The only flash of impatience in the dialogue, and it is on behalf of conversation. Told that arguing may cost him a harder death, he chooses the argument without a second's thought. Crito's 'I knew quite well what you would say' is the tired affection of a very old friend.

links.why: The first defence, which he now says he must improve on; there he was far less sure what death is.
The prisoner who 'has no right to open the door and run away' has already turned down Crito's plan of escape.
The idea that we are in the gods' service was left hanging in the Euthyphro, where nobody could say what that service is for.
The defence itself, which begins the moment Crito's interruption is brushed aside.

pha3.essay:
Here is the thesis that has made this dialogue famous and, to many readers, faintly repellent: the true philosopher 'is always pursuing death and dying'. Simmias laughs, because back home in Thebes people would say that philosophers are half dead already and deserve the rest. Socrates takes the joke and keeps it. Yes, he says, only they do not know what kind of death.

Watch the first step, because everything hangs on it and it goes by in two lines. 'Do we believe that there is such a thing as death?' 'Is it not the separation of soul and body?' Simmias says 'Just so'. But that definition already contains the conclusion. If death is a separation, then there are two things, and the soul is the sort of thing that can 'exist in herself' once apart. Anyone who thinks death is simply the end of a living creature has been ruled out before the argument begins. Socrates calls this a defence and not a proof, and Cebes will call the bluff the moment the speech ends, so I do not think Plato is cheating; but it is worth knowing where the weight rests.

From there the case is built in three layers. First, character: the philosopher does not care for food, drink, sex, 'costly raiment, or sandals'. Second, knowledge: the senses are 'inaccurate witnesses', and thought is best when the mind is 'gathered into herself'. Third, and almost in passing, the objects of knowledge: 'Is there or is there not an absolute justice?' 'Assuredly there is.' That quick exchange is the theory of Forms entering the dialogue, with no fanfare, as something this circle already takes for granted. Justice itself, beauty itself, the 'essence or true nature of everything': nobody has seen them with eyes, yet they are what we most want to know. If the real things are invisible and the body deals only in the visible, then the body is in the way, and a life spent thinking is a life spent loosening the tie that death cuts.

The long speech Socrates puts in the mouths of 'real philosophers' is the high-water mark of this hostility. The body fills us with 'loves, and lusts, and fears, and fancies of all kinds, and endless foolery'; wars are fought for money, and money is wanted for the body. I admire the rhetoric and resist the doctrine. It is a strange thing to hear from a man who a few pages ago was enjoying the feeling coming back into his leg, who has a child young enough to be carried in arms, and whose own philosophy was done in the marketplace, by talking, with ears and eyes. And there is a hinge in it that deserves suspicion: 'either knowledge is not to be attained at all, or, if at all, after death'. The first alternative is simply dropped. A sceptic would take it.

What does convince me is the passage on virtue, which could stand on its own. Ordinary courage, Socrates says, is fear in disguise: men face death because they fear something worse. Ordinary temperance is greed in disguise: people forgo some pleasures to keep others. So most virtue is a kind of money-changing, 'the exchange of one fear or pleasure or pain for another', and the only sound currency is wisdom. This is an acute piece of moral psychology, and it turns on anyone who behaves well for the reward, including the reward of heaven. I am not sure Socrates fully escapes his own net. A man who gives up pleasure now in the hope of wisdom hereafter looks as if he is trading too. His answer would be that wisdom is not one more good to be weighed against the others but the thing that makes any of them worth having. I half accept that.

The speech closes in the language of the mysteries: purification, initiation, the few true mystics among the many who carry the wand. Jowett's vocabulary helps the churchly tone along ('votary', 'repine', 'unsanctified'), and it is fair to notice how religious the philosophy has become. Yet the last note is pure Socrates: whether he has sought in the right way, 'I shall truly know in a little while'. Then he appeals to the verdict again, hoping to do better than he did before the Athenians. The jury's first response, from Cebes, opens [[pha4|the next section]], and it is not an acquittal.

annotations.quote: they do not perceive that he is always pursuing death and dying
annotations.note: The paradox stated at full strength, before any softening. What he turns out to mean is a habit of attention, withdrawing the mind from appetite and sensation, but he chooses the most shocking name for it on purpose, on the one day when the word 'death' cannot be heard as a figure of speech.

annotations.quote: Is it not the separation of soul and body?
annotations.note: The whole dialogue rests on this definition and Simmias waves it through. It assumes that the soul is a separable thing, which is exactly what remains to be shown. Keep it in mind when Simmias himself, in [[pha7]], proposes that the soul may be more like the tuning of an instrument.

annotations.quote: Is there or is there not an absolute justice?
annotations.note: The Forms arrive. Jowett's 'absolute' renders the Greek for justice 'itself', the thing all just acts have in common and none perfectly is. Note that nobody argues for it here; Simmias answers 'Assuredly'. Every later proof in the Phaedo borrows against this unargued agreement.

annotations.quote: Whence come wars, and fightings, and factions? whence but from the body and the lusts of the body?
annotations.note: A whole theory of history in one line: war comes from money and money from bodily want. It is too simple, since men fight for honour and for ideas as readily as for goods, but it is striking to hear it from a veteran of three Athenian campaigns.

annotations.quote: either knowledge is not to be attained at all, or, if at all, after death
annotations.note: A fork with two prongs, and Socrates walks down the second without looking at the first. The possibility that pure knowledge is just not available to creatures like us is left lying there. I think this is the weakest joint in the speech.

annotations.quote: Many a man has been willing to go to the world below animated by the hope of seeing there an earthly love, or wife, or son
annotations.note: He is thinking of stories like Orpheus going down for Eurydice. The comparison makes philosophy a love affair, which is what the word says: the philosopher is wisdom's lover, and will go where she is. It is also the one moment in the speech where wives and sons are allowed to matter.

annotations.quote: that a man should be courageous from fear, and because he is a coward, is surely a strange thing
annotations.note: The sharpest observation in the section. The soldier holds the line because he is more afraid of disgrace than of the enemy, so his courage is one fear beating another. Once this is seen, it is hard to stop seeing it.

annotations.quote: is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?
annotations.note: The image is of a money-changer's table. Swapping one pleasure for a bigger one is barter among counterfeits; wisdom is the only legal tender. The phrasing is slippery on whether wisdom is what you pay or what you buy, and I suspect the ambiguity is the point: with wisdom, the means and the end are the same thing.

annotations.quote: are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics
annotations.note: A saying from the cult of Dionysus: many carry the ritual wand, few are truly possessed by the god. Socrates annexes it for philosophy with a breezy 'as I interpret the words'. It is the ancestor of 'many are called, but few are chosen', and it shows how openly he is presenting philosophy as a rite of salvation.

links.why: In the Apology he said death was either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and did not claim to know which; compare that caution with the confidence here.
The 'practice of dying' comes back there with an argument behind it, and with a better account of what pleasure and pain do to the mind.
Cebes immediately points out what this speech assumed, and the proofs begin.
The Forms slipped in here as common ground become the engine of the recollection argument.

pha4.essay:
Cebes says what any honest listener must: all that was fine, but it assumes the soul survives. People fear that at death she goes out 'like smoke or air'. So the dialogue changes gear from defence to proof, and Socrates, with a glance at Aristophanes, remarks that nobody could now accuse him of chattering about things that do not concern him.

The first proof is the one from opposites, and I will say plainly that I think it is the weakest in the book. The principle is that opposites come from opposites: what becomes larger was smaller, what wakes was asleep. Life and death are opposites; the dead come from the living; therefore the living come from the dead, and the souls of the dead must be somewhere in the meantime. The trouble is in the slide from the examples to the case. When something small becomes large, one thing persists through the change and has first one property and then the other. To apply this to living and dead you must already suppose a persisting something that is first alive, then dead, then alive again, and that something is the soul, the very point in dispute. For a person who thinks death is the end, 'the dead' is not a condition that anyone is in. Cebes' answer, 'I can only say in answer--the living', has a reluctance in it that I like to think is deliberate.

The supporting argument is better and stranger. If dying were a one-way street, all things would 'at last be swallowed up in death'; nature would 'walk on one leg only'. This is really a thought about conservation, that the world's stock of life must be recycled or run out, and it has a certain grandeur. But it only works if nothing new ever comes to be alive, and Socrates waves that possibility away in half a sentence. It also proves a good deal more than he needs: the argument is explicitly about 'animals generally, and plants', so every beetle and fig tree has its soul waiting below.

Still, notice what Socrates got from the fetters that morning in [[pha1]]: pleasure following pain, joined at the head. He has been thinking in cycles since he sat up. And he does not rest on this proof. Cebes at once offers a second, [[pha5|recollection]], Socrates will lean the two against each other, and after that the argument from opposites is heard of very little.

annotations.quote: issuing forth dispersed like smoke or air and in her flight vanishing away into nothingness
annotations.note: The picture every later argument is trying to dispel. In Greek the soul, psyche, is by origin a word for breath, so the fear that it simply blows away is built into the language. Cebes attributes it politely to 'men' in general.

annotations.quote: not even if he were one of my old enemies, the Comic poets, could accuse me of idle talking
annotations.note: Aristophanes had put a 'Socrates' on stage dangling in a basket and prattling about the heavens, and in [[ap1]] Socrates blames that caricature for much of the prejudice against him. On the day of his death, talk about the soul can hardly be called a matter in which he has no concern. It is a dry, slightly bitter joke.

annotations.quote: Are not all things which have opposites generated out of their opposites?
annotations.note: Everything depends on what 'generated out of' means. A bigger thing comes from a smaller in the sense that the same thing was smaller before. Whether a living person 'comes from' a dead one in that sense is the question, and the phrasing hides it.

annotations.quote: I can only say in answer--the living.
annotations.note: Cebes is the sharpest person in the room, and this is not the voice of a man persuaded so much as a man who sees where the questions have boxed him in. Jowett's dash catches the pause.

annotations.quote: And shall we suppose nature to walk on one leg only?
annotations.note: A memorable image doing the work of a premise. Why should nature not be lame? Plenty of processes run one way only: we grow old and do not grow young. The appeal is to symmetry, and symmetry is something we hope for, which is not a proof that it is there.

annotations.quote: the tale of the sleeping Endymion would in the end have no meaning
annotations.note: Endymion was the beautiful youth granted eternal sleep. Socrates' point is that sleep is only remarkable against a background of waking; if everything slept, nobody would tell his story. It is a witty way of saying that a universe running one way would long since have run down.

annotations.quote: must not all things at last be swallowed up in death?
annotations.note: The strongest moment of the argument, and one that still has a pull. But the bracketed '(But compare Republic.)' that follows is Jowett's own cross-reference, not Plato's text: he is nudging the reader toward a passage where Plato argues the number of souls is fixed, the assumption this argument needs and does not state.

annotations.quote: and that the good souls have a better portion than the evil
annotations.note: Look how much has been added to the conclusion. Even if the argument worked, it would show only that souls go round; nothing in it distinguishes good from bad. Socrates' hope has outrun his proof by a clause.

links.why: The fable of pleasure and pain fastened by one head is this argument in miniature.
The second proof, which Socrates will prop against this one to cover the gap each leaves.
Opposites return in the final argument, where someone objects that Socrates now seems to be saying the reverse of what he said here.

pha5.essay:
Cebes introduces this argument as Socrates' 'favorite doctrine', and Simmias makes the dialogue's best small joke about it: he would like the doctrine of recollection 'brought to my own recollection'. The version Cebes sketches, questions and a diagram, is the slave-boy scene of [[me1|the Meno]]. What Socrates gives here is a new and deeper version, and I think it is the philosophical centre of this half of the dialogue, so it is worth taking slowly.

He starts with ordinary reminding. A lover sees a lyre and thinks of the boy who plays it; you see a portrait of Simmias and think of Simmias. One thing calls up another that was already known. Then the turn: sometimes the reminder is like the thing recalled, and when it is, we can ask how far it falls short. Now take two sticks that look equal. They look equal at one time and unequal at another, from one angle and not from the next. But equality itself is never inequality. So the sticks and 'absolute equality' are different things. And when we look at the sticks we judge them against it: they 'strive to attain absolute equality, but fall short of it'. To judge that a thing falls short of a standard, you must already possess the standard. We have been making such judgments since we first opened our eyes. So we had the standard before we first opened our eyes: 'before we were born, I suppose?'

There is something here that I think is simply true and important. We do possess notions, perfect equality, the exact circle, justice without remainder, that nothing in experience ever fully instantiates, and we use them to measure experience. Where they come from is a real question, and the long quarrel between those who say the mind brings its own furniture and those who say it is furnished by the senses starts on this page. What I do not accept is that Socrates has closed off the alternatives. He says himself, more than once, that we got the idea of equality 'from' seeing equal sticks and stones, and could have got it no other way. But if experience is enough to prompt the idea, why can it not be enough to form it? We see things more and less alike and extend the series in thought to its limit; on that account the ideal is an extrapolation and not a memory. Socrates needs the sense of falling short to come first, and he never shows that it does.

Simmias then makes exactly the right objection, and I wish he had held to it: perhaps these notions 'are given us at the very moment of birth'. Socrates replies that we should then have to lose them at the same instant, since infants plainly cannot give an account of equality. Simmias collapses: 'I was unconsciously talking nonsense'. He was not. There is a third possibility between knowing something outright and having forgotten it, which is to be so made that one will come to see it, as we are born without teeth but not without the makings of them. Plato's choice between knowledge kept and knowledge lost leaves no room for a capacity, and a capacity needs no previous life.

Two more things, both to Plato's credit. He states the dependency out loud: the proof stands only if the Forms exist, 'and if not the ideas, then not the souls'. Everything is being staked on one hypothesis, and [[phb1|the second half]] will stake still more on it. And he lets the listeners count what has been bought. Simmias and Cebes agree that at most 'about half of what was required has been proven': the soul existed before birth, and nothing follows about afterwards. Socrates' patch, adding this argument to [[pha4|the one from opposites]], is no stronger than that earlier argument, and his manner suggests he knows it.

Because here the tone changes, and for me this is the most moving page so far. He teases them: you are afraid, like children, that the wind will scatter the soul, 'especially if a man should happen to die in a great storm'. Cebes smiles and owns it, not quite for himself but for the 'child within us to whom death is a sort of hobgoblin'. The cure prescribed is not a proof but a charm, to be sung daily. Simmias has already let slip that by this time tomorrow no one alive will be able to give a proper account of these things; now Cebes says it to his face, asking where they will find such a charmer 'when you are gone'. Socrates answers that Greece is a large place, and that they must search among themselves. He takes the plainest mention yet of his death and uses it to hand the work on.

annotations.quote: Your favorite doctrine, Socrates, that knowledge is simply recollection
annotations.note: Plato is pointing back at his own earlier dialogue; Jowett even inserts '(Compare Meno.)' a few lines on to make sure nobody misses it. In [[me1]] the doctrine is drawn out of a slave boy and a geometry problem. Here it is treated as a familiar house view, which tells us this is written for readers who know the earlier book.

annotations.quote: I want to have this doctrine of recollection brought to my own recollection
annotations.note: Simmias has forgotten the argument that all learning is remembering, and asks to be reminded of it. The joke is light, but it also quietly performs the thesis: he half knows it, and questions will bring it back.

annotations.quote: form in the mind's eye an image of the youth to whom the lyre belongs
annotations.note: The first example of recollection is a love story: an object that brings its owner to mind. I think that is chosen with care. The claim to come is that every equal pair of sticks is a keepsake of something we once knew and miss. And a lyre will matter again, in other hands, in [[pha7]].

annotations.quote: Say so, yes, replied Simmias, and swear to it, with all the confidence in life.
annotations.note: The existence of equality 'itself' is the premise the whole proof needs, and it is granted with an oath instead of a reason. Simmias is a believer in the Forms before the argument starts. A reader who is not should notice that nothing here was meant to convert him.

annotations.quote: Do not the same pieces of wood or stone appear at one time equal, and at another time unequal?
annotations.note: The crux, and a famously unclear sentence in the Greek, which may mean equal to one person and not another, or to one thing and not another. Either way the contrast holds: any sensible pair is equal only in a qualified, wobbling way, whereas equality is never also its opposite.

annotations.quote: all these apparent equals strive to attain absolute equality, but fall short of it
annotations.note: Sticks do not strive. The language of aiming and failing is a metaphor carrying a great deal of weight, since the argument needs us to experience ordinary things as attempts at something better. I do recognise the experience; whether it is a memory is another matter.

annotations.quote: to-morrow, at this time, there will no longer be any one alive who is able to give an account of them
annotations.note: In the middle of an abstract exchange about who can define equality, Simmias suddenly remembers what day it is. It is the highest compliment paid to Socrates in the dialogue, and it comes as a slip. Socrates does not acknowledge it and goes straight on.

annotations.quote: and if not the ideas, then not the souls
annotations.note: An unusually clean statement of what depends on what. The pre-existence of the soul is exactly as secure as the Forms and no more. Plato is not hiding his foundation; he is telling us where to push.

annotations.quote: there is a child within us to whom death is a sort of hobgoblin
annotations.note: Cebes puts his finger on why proofs do not settle this. The reasoning adult may be convinced while something younger inside stays frightened of the dark. Jowett's 'hobgoblin' is a nursery word from his own century and exactly right for the Greek bogey. Socrates' answer, that the child needs a charm sung to it daily, concedes that argument alone is not enough.

links.why: Recollection is first argued in the Meno, with the slave boy and the diagram Cebes alludes to; this is the sequel and the revision.
The 'absolute' justice and beauty that Simmias granted so quickly there are the standards this argument says we were born remembering.
'Holiness' is on the list of things whose essence we knew before birth; the Euthyphro is a whole dialogue failing to recollect it.
Recollection is the one argument everyone still accepts after the objections, and Socrates uses it there as a lever against Simmias.

pha6.essay:
Having promised a charm, Socrates produces what is usually called the affinity argument, and it behaves more like a charm than a proof. What kind of thing gets scattered? Compound things, which can come apart as they were put together. What is safe? The uncompounded, which is also the unchanging. The Forms are like that: invisible, constant, grasped only by the mind. Bodies are the reverse. And the soul? She is invisible; she is steadied when she thinks about steady things; she rules while the body obeys. So she is 'more like' the divine and indissoluble, and the body is like the mortal.

The honest word in all this is 'almost'. The soul is 'almost or altogether indissoluble', and an argument from likeness can never deliver more than that. Resembling an indestructible thing in some respects does not make one indestructible, and one of the respects is shaky: 'not seen', Cebes carefully says, 'by man'. Plenty of things are invisible and perish. Worse, the passage undermines its own premise as it goes. The soul is supposed to be changeless, yet we are told that she 'wanders and is confused', reels 'like a drunkard', can be 'polluted', made 'heavy and weighty and earthy', nailed and riveted. A thing so thoroughly altered by the company it keeps is not obviously simple. I read the resemblance to the Forms less as a fact about the soul than as a task set for her, and I suspect Plato does too, since [[pha7|Simmias and Cebes]] are about to take the argument apart with his full cooperation.

Then proof gives way to preaching, and the preaching is wonderful. Souls too fond of the body hang about graveyards, 'cloyed with sight' (Jowett cannot resist pasting in a dozen lines of Milton); gluttons come back as asses, tyrants as wolves and kites, and the decent, unphilosophical citizen as a bee, a wasp or an ant. I cannot believe Socrates says the last with a straight face. Respectable habit earns the hive.

One passage in the sermon I take entirely seriously. The worst evil of strong pleasure and pain, he says, is that whatever causes them seems at that moment 'plainest and truest'. Each one is 'a sort of nail' fixing the soul to the body's account of what is real. That seems to me exact, whatever becomes of immortality: intensity passes itself off as evidence. The practice described in [[pha3]] as dying looks more attractive here, as a refusal to let the loudest feeling decide what is true.

annotations.quote: that which is uncompounded, and that only, must be, if anything is, indissoluble
annotations.note: A reasonable principle: what has no parts cannot fall to pieces. But note what it leaves open. A simple thing might end in some other way than by coming apart, by fading, say, or by being used up, and that is the gap Cebes will find in [[pha7]].

annotations.quote: the world spins round her, and she is like a drunkard, when she touches change
annotations.note: A vivid picture of the mind lost among sensations, and awkward for the argument it sits in. If the soul can be made dizzy by what she attends to, she is not unchanging in the way the Forms are. Her steadiness is borrowed from her objects, in both directions.

annotations.quote: and is not the soul almost or altogether indissoluble?
annotations.note: The two words that matter are 'almost or'. Socrates is too honest to claim the argument gives more, and Cebes, who says 'Certainly', has heard the hedge. An almost-immortal soul is precisely what his weaver will describe.

annotations.quote: For is not philosophy the practice of death?
annotations.note: The slogan from [[pha3]], now with a theory under it: thinking gathers the soul 'herself into herself', which is what death does all at once. In Jowett's text Cebes breaks in with 'Certainly--' before the sentence is finished, as if he had been waiting for the phrase to come round.

annotations.quote: The soul grows clotted by contagion, Imbodies, and imbrutes
annotations.note: This is not Plato. Jowett, an Oxford clergyman translating for Victorian readers, interrupts the Greek to quote Milton's Comus, which was itself modelled on this very passage. It is a fair sample of how his generation read the Phaedo, as near-Christian scripture, and a reminder that the translation has an accent of its own.

annotations.quote: such as bees or wasps or ants, or back again into the form of man
annotations.note: The reward for conventional good behaviour 'without philosophy and mind' is to come back as a social insect. Orderly, industrious, and incapable of a thought: I take it as satire on civic respectability, and one of the driest jokes in the dialogue.

annotations.quote: she could only view real existence through the bars of a prison
annotations.note: Said in a prison, by a prisoner. The harder twist comes in the same sentence: the soul is 'the principal accomplice in her own captivity'. The body does not hold us; our wanting does. Plato is already sketching the cave he will build in the Republic.

annotations.quote: each pleasure and pain is a sort of nail which nails and rivets the soul to the body
annotations.note: The best image in the section, and the claim behind it is precise. The harm of intense feeling is not the hangover or the lost money but the conviction it produces that its object is the realest thing there is. I think this survives the collapse of everything else in the argument.

annotations.quote: weaving instead of unweaving her Penelope's web
annotations.note: Penelope unpicked by night what she wove by day to put off her suitors. A soul that uses philosophy to get free and then hands herself back to pleasure is doing the same futile labour in reverse. Within a page Cebes will bring a weaver of his own, to less comforting effect.

links.why: The first statement of philosophy as a rehearsal for death, which this section tries to ground in the soul's nature.
Both objections aim squarely at this argument: one at 'invisible and divine', the other at 'almost indissoluble'.
The fate of pure and impure souls, sketched here with asses and wolves, is drawn at full scale in the closing myth.

pha7.essay:
The silence after the sermon is one of Plato's great stage directions. Everyone is thinking; two Thebans are whispering; and it is Socrates who breaks in to say that the argument has 'many points still open to suspicion and attack'. A man with hours to live invites the demolition of his comfort, and when Simmias hesitates out of delicacy, he answers with the swans. People say they sing in grief before they die; Socrates says they sing for joy, being Apollo's birds, and that he is their 'fellow-servant'. The poet of the hymn to Apollo in [[pha2]] is still at work.

Simmias prefaces his objection with what I think is the most honest account of belief in the dialogue. Certainty on these matters is 'hard or rather impossible' in this life; it would be cowardly not to test every account; and failing truth, one should take the best available human theory 'and let this be the raft upon which he sails through life'. That is not Socrates' confidence, and it is closer to where most of us live.

His objection is devastatingly neat. Everything said about the soul, that it is invisible, incorporeal, divine, can be said of the tuning of a lyre, and nobody thinks the tuning outlasts the smashed instrument. Perhaps the soul is the body's attunement, the right tension of hot and cold, wet and dry. Change the vocabulary and this is the commonest modern view: mind is what a properly organised body does. Cebes grants more and asks for more. Let the soul be tougher than the body; let her outlast many bodies as a weaver outlasts many coats; the last coat still survives the weaver. Durability is not immortality, and the earlier arguments at best showed durability. Nothing short of proof that the soul is 'altogether immortal and imperishable' will do.

Both objections seem to me entirely fair, and it matters that Plato wrote them. He gives his opponents better images than his hero has yet had, and he has Socrates smile and say that Simmias 'has reason on his side'. Then Phaedo reports the effect in the room: not disagreement but vertigo, the fear that there are 'no grounds of belief' in any argument at all. That, more than mortality, is the danger the dialogue now faces, and it is the first thing Socrates turns to in [[phb1|the second half]]. Whether his replies succeed is for that half to judge. My own view is that the answer to Simmias is clever and the answer to Cebes magnificent and unfinished; but the questions were the right ones.

annotations.quote: there are many points still open to suspicion and attack
annotations.note: Nobody has objected yet. Socrates raises the doubt himself, after what sounded like a triumphant close. It is the clearest sign that the sermon in [[pha6]] was never meant to be the last word, and that he would sooner be refuted than humoured.

annotations.quote: would not go out of life less merrily than the swans
annotations.note: The origin of the 'swan song', with its meaning reversed: the popular notion is a lament, and Socrates insists it is a song of gladness that men mishear because they project their own fear onto the bird. It is a small lesson in how fear distorts evidence, slipped in as natural history.

annotations.quote: let this be the raft upon which he sails through life
annotations.note: My favourite image in this half. A raft is something lashed together from what is to hand, good enough to keep afloat and known to be less than a ship. Simmias does allow for 'some word of God' that might carry one more safely, but he does not claim to have it. This is how a thoughtful doubter lives.

annotations.quote: then the soul is the harmony or due proportionate admixture of them
annotations.note: The theory in a sentence. Jowett's 'harmony' means tuning, the right tension of the strings, not a melody. On this view the soul is real and even 'divine', but it is a state of the body and cannot exist without it. It was a serious medical and Pythagorean idea, and with 'brain' for 'body' it still is.

annotations.quote: Socrates looked fixedly at us as his manner was, and said with a smile
annotations.note: Phaedo remembers the look. The famous Socratic stare, then a smile, then the admission that the attack has force and the mischievous suggestion that someone else answer it. He is visibly enjoying himself, which is its own kind of argument about how to meet death.

annotations.quote: see, there is the coat which he himself wove and wore, and which remains whole and undecayed
annotations.note: Cebes parodies the reasoning of the affinity argument: the coat outlived the man, the man is more durable than a coat, so the man must still be alive. Put that way it is plainly absurd. The image also turns Penelope's web from the previous page to a darker use: here the weaver wears out.

annotations.quote: she will weary in the labours of successive births, and may at last succumb in one of her deaths
annotations.note: The most unsettling thought in the first half. Cebes accepts pre-existence, accepts even reincarnation, and asks why a soul that has lasted a long time should last for ever. For all anyone can tell, this death might be the one that finishes her. Every earlier argument slides past this.

annotations.quote: either we were incapable of forming a judgment, or there were no grounds of belief
annotations.note: The real crisis is here. They were convinced and are now unconvinced, and the natural conclusion is to distrust conviction itself. Plato halts the story at this point, with Echecrates breaking in from the frame at the opening of [[phb1]] to say he feels it too.

links.why: The argument under attack: Simmias borrows its list of the soul's attributes and Cebes its 'almost indissoluble'.
Cebes still accepts recollection and pre-existence in full, which is what makes his objection so hard to shake off.
The replies begin there, after a warning against hating argument that is addressed to exactly the mood this section ends in.

phb1.essay:
The dialogue stops. Echecrates, who has been a silent listener since the first page, breaks in to say what I was thinking: 'What argument can I ever trust again?' It is a shrewd piece of staging. Plato has let the objections of Simmias and Cebes land so hard ([[pha1|the first half]] ends on them) that even the man hearing the story at second hand, weeks later and miles away, has lost his nerve. So before any reply comes, we are made to feel the room.

What Socrates does first is not argue. He plays with Phaedo's hair. The hair will be cut tomorrow in mourning, and he says: cut it today, if we let the argument die. It is the tenderest moment so far, and it is also a redefinition of what there is to grieve. A dead friend is one thing; a dead argument is worse.

Then the warning, which I think is the most durable thing in the Phaedo, and which would survive the failure of every proof in it. Jowett's 'misologists' are haters of argument, and Socrates explains them by the people who hate mankind. You trust too easily, you are let down, you are let down again, and you conclude that nobody is any good. The disappointed truster does the same with reasoning, and ends up proud of it, one of the 'great disputers' who alone have seen that nothing holds. The cure in both cases is the same piece of experience: the fault was in your trusting, not in the whole class of things you trusted. 'Rather say that we have not yet attained to soundness in ourselves.' Notice the small stumble where he admits the comparison ran away with him: bad arguments, unlike bad men, are not rare.

And then he says something I did not expect. He is not, today, a philosopher. 'Like the vulgar, I am only a partisan.' He wants this conclusion to be true, he knows he wants it, and he tells the two young men to resist him 'might and main' for exactly that reason. There is even a little wager folded in: if he is right, good; if there is nothing after death, at least he will not have spent the afternoon wailing. I find this more persuasive than anything that follows, and it is worth carrying forward as a standard. The man conducting the proof has told us he is not to be trusted with it. He has asked to be checked. I intend to take him up on it.

annotations.quote: What argument can I ever trust again?
annotations.note: The frame breaks in for the first time since the opening. Echecrates is not in the prison; he is hearing this later, in another city, and the objections have shaken him anyway. Plato is telling us the doubt is meant to be ours too.

annotations.quote: He might be compared to a general rallying his defeated and broken army
annotations.note: A military figure for a man about to lose everything. What Phaedo admires is not that Socrates had an answer but that he saw the damage done to his listeners and attended to it first.

annotations.quote: he had a way of playing with my hair
annotations.note: One of the few physical habits of Socrates that Plato records, and it comes from the narrator's own memory of being touched. Phaedo will cut this hair tomorrow in mourning. The argument that follows about what deserves mourning starts from here.

annotations.quote: I will be your Iolaus until the sun goes down
annotations.note: Iolaus was the nephew who helped Heracles when one monster became two. The joke is light, but 'until the sun goes down' is the deadline of the execution, dropped in without emphasis.

annotations.quote: few are the good and few the evil, and that the great majority are in the interval between them
annotations.note: A piece of plain worldly sense in the middle of a metaphysical dialogue. The misanthrope's error is statistical: he met a few bad cases and inferred the whole population.

annotations.quote: like the currents in the Euripus, are going up and down in never-ceasing ebb and flow
annotations.note: The Euripus is the narrow strait between Euboea and the mainland, notorious for reversing its current several times a day. It is the picture of a mind that has decided nothing can be settled, and takes that for sophistication.

annotations.quote: like the vulgar, I am only a partisan
annotations.note: The most disarming sentence in the dialogue. On the day it matters most he admits he is arguing for the side he needs to win. Everything he proves after this should be read with the admission in mind, which is what he asks for.

annotations.quote: and like the bee, leave my sting in you before I die
annotations.note: At his trial he called himself a gadfly that stings Athens awake. Here the insect is one that dies of its own sting, and the sting is a false belief left behind in friends. He would rather lose the argument than do that.

links.why: The objections of Simmias and Cebes that produced this despair are at the end of the first half.
The stinging insect appears at the trial too, as the gadfly, and the comparison shows how his tone has changed.
The proof he asks us to resist 'might and main' is here, and Simmias takes him at his word.

phb2.essay:
Three replies to Simmias, and they are not equally good. I will take them in order, because Socrates moves fast here and Simmias gives up faster.

The first is a trap built from Simmias's own commitments. He still believes that learning is recollection ([[me1|the Meno]] is where that idea gets its demonstration), so the soul existed before the body. But a tuning cannot exist before the lyre it is the tuning of. One of the two beliefs has to go, and Simmias drops harmony at once, calling it merely 'probable and plausible.' Fair enough, but see how little this proves. It refutes Simmias, not the theory. Anyone who doubts recollection keeps the harmony view intact, and it is still the nearest ancient relative of what most people now believe about minds and brains.

The second reply I cannot make come out. A harmony can be more or less of a harmony; a soul is not more or less of a soul; virtue is a kind of harmony; so if the soul were a harmony, all souls would be equally good, or we would need a harmony inside a harmony. The steps slide between being a tuning and being well tuned. A lyre badly tuned is still tuned to something, and nobody thinks that makes all lyres equal. Simmias's 'I cannot tell' is the honest answer.

The third is the one with force. A tuning follows the strings; it cannot push back against them. But the soul does push back: thirsty, we refuse to drink. Socrates quotes Odysseus scolding his own heart, 'as if talking to a thing which is not herself.' Something in us commands, and a mere arrangement of parts does not give orders to the parts. I feel the weight of this. Still, the modern answer is easy to state: one part of the arrangement is checking another. Plato himself, in the Republic, will use this same line of Homer to show a conflict within the soul, between reason and anger, which rather spoils its use here as soul against body.

Then a Theban joke. Harmonia was the wife of Cadmus, founder of Thebes; having appeased the lady, Socrates turns to the husband, and Cebes is the harder case. His restatement of Cebes's worry is scrupulous, and it includes the grimmest phrase in the dialogue: the soul's very entry into a body 'may be a sort of disease which is the beginning of dissolution.' Keep that image of life as sickness in mind. It has not finished with us.

annotations.quote: you will have to think differently, my Theban friend
annotations.note: The whole first reply is in this sentence. Simmias has just said he cannot imagine giving up recollection, and Socrates points out that he must then give up something else he holds. It is a refutation of a person's set of beliefs, not yet of the harmony theory itself.

annotations.quote: there surely ought to be harmony in a discourse of which harmony is the theme
annotations.note: A pun, and a principle. Socrates' test for a position is always whether its parts can be held together, and here he gets to say so in the theory's own vocabulary.

annotations.quote: I know too well that these arguments from probabilities are impostors
annotations.note: Simmias disowns his own objection as merely likely-sounding. I think he sells it short. An analogy that fits the facts as well as the lyre does is not nothing, and 'in geometry' shows what standard he is measuring by: proof or nothing.

annotations.quote: is one soul in the very least degree more or less, or more or less completely, a soul than another?
annotations.note: The premise that drives the second reply. It sounds obvious, but it is carrying a great deal: it treats 'soul' as an all-or-nothing kind, like 'three', which is the very thing a harmony theorist would deny.

annotations.quote: all souls of all living creatures will be equally good?
annotations.note: The absurd conclusion meant to sink the theory. I do not think it follows. That every lyre is tuned somehow does not make every lyre in tune, and the argument needs those two to be the same.

annotations.quote: as if talking to a thing which is not herself
annotations.note: The real argument, in eight words. We address our appetites, bargain with them, overrule them. Whatever does the overruling does not look like a by-product of the thing overruled.

annotations.quote: Endure, my heart; far worse hast thou endured
annotations.note: Odysseus, back in his own house in disguise, holding down his rage until the moment is right. Homer is called as a witness to a point of psychology. Jowett gives him the 'hast thou' of an English epic.

annotations.quote: may be a sort of disease which is the beginning of dissolution
annotations.note: This is Socrates restating Cebes, not speaking for himself, and the distinction matters. The idea that being born is the start of an illness will be in the air at the very end, and it is worth remembering whose image it was.

links.why: Simmias's lyre and Cebes's weaver are set out in full at the close of the first half; reread them before judging the replies.
The first reply rests entirely on recollection, and the Meno is where that doctrine is argued for with the slave and the square.
The answer to Cebes, promised here, is the final argument, and it quietly assumes the harmony view is dead.

phb3.essay:
'Socrates paused awhile.' It is the only long silence in the dialogue, and what comes out of it is not an argument but a life story. Cebes has asked whether the soul can wear out, and Socrates answers that this means settling how anything at all comes to be or ceases, and that he had better say how he came to think about causes the way he does. For once we are told where the method came from.

As a young man, he says, he was mad for natural science: whether we think with blood or air or the brain, how animals grow, what holds the earth up. The result was that he unlearned things he thought he knew. His examples sound childish and are not. If putting one beside one is what makes two, and cutting one in half is also what makes two, then opposite processes yield the same result, and neither can be what two-ness consists in. He is asking what would count as an explanation, and deciding that a recipe for producing a thing is not an account of what it is.

Then Anaxagoras, heard read aloud, saying that Mind orders everything. The paragraph of hope that follows is lovely, a young man planning the questions he will ask his book: is the earth flat or round, and why is that best? And the book lets him down. Mind is named and then dropped in favour of 'air, and ether, and water, and other eccentricities.'

Here comes the passage I would save if I could keep only one page of Plato. Why is Socrates sitting in this cell? You could answer with bones, joints and muscles. All true, all necessary, and all beside the point, because the same bones 'would have gone off long ago to Megara or Boeotia' had he not judged it better to stay. The whole of [[cr1|the Crito]] is packed into that joke; the escape was arranged, and the legs were willing. A reason is not one more part in the machine. Without the bones he could not act, but they are the condition and not the cause.

I believe that distinction and I think it is permanent. What I do not believe is the extension he wanted. That Socrates sits because he thinks it best is one thing; that the earth sits where it does because that is best is quite another, and the science that actually succeeded is the kind Anaxagoras wrote, air and ether and all. To his credit Socrates does not claim to have found the better kind. He 'failed either to discover myself, or to learn of any one else,' and what he offers instead he calls second best.

The second best is a retreat from things to statements about them, pictured as watching an eclipse in a reflection so as not to go blind. Jowett slips in 'through a glass darkly,' which is St Paul in the King James Bible and not Plato, but the point survives: Socrates denies that thinking is a dimmer view than looking. The procedure is to lay down the strongest assumption you have, keep what agrees with it, and defend it only by climbing to a higher assumption. Readers of [[me1|the Meno]] have seen a first sketch of this. The assumption he chooses is that there is such a thing as beauty itself, and that beautiful things are beautiful by sharing in it, 'in whatever way or manner obtained; for as to the manner I am uncertain.'

It is fair to feel cheated. 'By beauty beautiful things become beautiful' sounds like no answer at all, and he half says so himself: 'simply and singly, and perhaps foolishly.' The joke about the man who is taller 'by a head,' so that a small thing makes him large, is a pun on the word 'by' and I do not think it deserves Cebes's laugh. But the safe answer earns its keep as a rule about what explanations must not do. They must not cite a cause that could as easily produce the opposite. That is a real constraint, and the proof of immortality in [[phb4|the next section]] is built from nothing else.

One doubt about the history. In [[ap1|the Apology]] Socrates tells the jury he has 'nothing to do with physical speculations.' A youthful phase would square the two, but the theory he arrives at here sounds to me like Plato's own, lent to his teacher on the last day. And when Echecrates breaks in again, this time to praise the 'wonderful clearness' of it all, I confess I smile. Clear is not the word I would have chosen.

annotations.quote: Socrates paused awhile, and seemed to be absorbed in reflection
annotations.note: He has answered everything so far without a pause. Cebes's objection is the one that makes him stop, and Phaedo thought the silence worth reporting. What follows is the longest stretch of uninterrupted speech from Socrates in the dialogue.

annotations.quote: I had a prodigious desire to know that department of philosophy which is called the investigation of nature
annotations.note: A Socrates we have not met: a young enthusiast for what we would call physics and physiology. The questions he lists, including whether the brain is the seat of perception, were the live scientific disputes of the fifth century.

annotations.quote: for then a different cause would produce the same effect
annotations.note: The hinge of the whole autobiography. Addition makes two and division makes two, so neither process can be what makes two two. From here on he will refuse any explanation that fails this test.

annotations.quote: These hopes I would not have sold for a large sum of money
annotations.note: The pitch of the young man's excitement, set up so the fall will be felt. What he hoped for was an account of the world in which 'why' always meant 'because it is best so'.

annotations.quote: would have gone off long ago to Megara or Boeotia--by the dog they would
annotations.note: Megara and Boeotia are the nearest borders, where his friends had offered to take him. 'By the dog' is Socrates' own odd oath. His legs, left to their own idea of the good, would have run.

annotations.quote: I wonder that they cannot distinguish the cause from the condition
annotations.note: A distinction philosophy has never stopped using: what makes a thing happen, as against what must be in place for it to happen. Bones are needed for sitting. They do not explain why he sits here and not in Megara.

annotations.quote: sees them only 'through a glass darkly,' any more than he who considers them in action and operation
annotations.note: The Biblical phrase is the translator's, and it colours the passage more than it should. The claim underneath is bold: studying things in reasoned statements is no more second-hand than studying them by sight.

annotations.quote: but I stoutly contend that by beauty all beautiful things become beautiful
annotations.note: The 'safe answer'. He will not say how a beautiful thing is related to beauty itself, only that the relation is what does the explaining. It is the theory of Forms at its most modest, and he sounds almost embarrassed by how little it says.

annotations.quote: Any one who has the least sense will acknowledge the wonderful clearness of Socrates' reasoning.
annotations.note: The second interruption from the frame. The first came at the moment of despair; this one comes at the laying of the foundation. Plato marks the place where he wants us to agree, which is usually a reason to slow down.

links.why: The 'true cause' of his sitting here, the decision not to escape, is argued out at length in the prison with Crito.
At his trial Socrates denies any interest in natural science; set that beside this account of his youth.
The method of reasoning from an assumption is first tried in the Meno, on the question whether virtue can be taught.
The 'safe answer' is immediately upgraded into the machinery of the final proof.

phb4.essay:
This is the proof the whole day has been building to, and I want to say exactly where it works and where it stops working, because Socrates comes close to telling us himself.

The machinery is patient. Simmias is tall beside Socrates and short beside Phaedo, but the tallness in him never becomes shortness; when the opposite comes, it must 'retire or perish.' Someone unnamed objects that this contradicts the earlier claim that opposites come from opposites ([[pha1]]), and gets a courteous, exact answer: then we meant things that have opposites, now the opposites themselves. Next, some things always carry one of a pair. Three is not the opposite of even, but three is always odd, and will 'endure annihilation or anything' sooner than be an even three. Fire always brings heat, snow cold. This licenses a cleverer kind of answer than the 'safe and stupid' one from [[phb3]]: what makes a body hot? Fire. What makes a body alive? Soul.

So soul always brings life, life's opposite is death, and soul will no more admit death than three admits the even. There is no such thing as a dead soul. Up to here I am persuaded, and it is a neat thing to have shown.

But look at the options that were on the table all along: retire or perish. Snow does not march off intact when the heat arrives. It melts. To get from 'a soul is never dead' to 'a soul never ceases' Socrates needs the soul to be the kind of thing that withdraws, and he sees this plainly: 'some other proof of her imperishableness will have to be given.' Cebes supplies it in one breath. If the immortal could perish, nothing would be imperishable. That only works if 'immortal' already means everlasting, which is the thing to be proved. A fire never admits cold either, and fires go out. The argument turns on two senses of one word, deathless while it lasts and lasting for ever, and I do not think the gap is closed.

There is a deeper assumption too: that the soul is a thing which arrives carrying life, rather than simply being the life of a body. That is Simmias's harmony again ([[phb2]]), and it was dismissed rather than buried.

What redeems the passage is its ending. Cebes is satisfied. Simmias cannot find a hole and still will not pretend to certainty, 'when I think of the greatness of the subject and the feebleness of man.' And Socrates, who warned us against his own partisanship in [[phb1]], says he is right: go back over the first principles. Plato could have ended on a triumph and chose to end on a reservation.

annotations.quote: He added, laughing, I am speaking like a book
annotations.note: He has just produced a sentence of comparative heights precise enough for a contract, and he hears himself. The care is needed, though: the proof depends on separating Simmias from the tallness in Simmias.

annotations.quote: either the greater will fly or retire before the opposite
annotations.note: Mark the two possibilities offered here, withdrawing or ceasing to exist. Both stay open through every example that follows. The conclusion will need one of them quietly dropped.

annotations.quote: though I do not exactly remember which of them
annotations.note: The best objection in the section comes from someone Phaedo cannot name. I like that Plato gives it to nobody in particular: it is the objection any attentive listener would raise, having heard the argument from opposites that morning.

annotations.quote: and yet I cannot deny that I am often disturbed by objections
annotations.note: Cebes in one line: not shaken now, but honest that he often is. After the warning against hating argument, this is what a healthy relation to objections sounds like.

annotations.quote: Will not the number three endure annihilation or anything sooner than be converted into an even number
annotations.note: The model case. Three and even are not opposites, yet three can never be even, because three always brings oddness with it. Notice that 'annihilation' is named as something three might undergo instead.

annotations.quote: this is what I call the safe and stupid answer
annotations.note: Socrates turning on his own safe answer a few pages after cherishing it. 'Heat makes things hot' is replaced by 'fire makes things hot': a thing that always carries the quality. The soul is about to be cast as the fire of life.
